stem: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of hypertension is seen in the outpatient clinic. His investigations revealed a Cr of 280 μmol/l, urinalysis of blood++ and urine protein of 1.8 g/l. Ultrasound scan of kidneys showed left kidney 9.5 cm and right kidney 9.9 cm. Which one of the following is the best investigation to diagnose the cause of his renal impairment?
explanation:
Renal biopsy
Proteinuria and haematuria are indicative of glomerulonephritis. There is a long history of hypertension and deranged renal function, which is compatible with a possible diagnosis of membranous glomerulonephritis. A significant number of cases of membranous glomerulonephritis are idiopathic. There is a preponderance of male cases, and presentation is most common in adulthood. The best way to establish the underlying diagnosis is via renal biopsy. Basement membrane thickening caused by immune complex deposition is the main feature of membranous glomerulonephritis. Associations include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), bowel and bronchus malignancy, penicillamine therapy and hepatitis B infection. Approximately one-third of patients develop kidney disease within 10–20 years of diagnosis. Patients with heavy proteinuria and progressive renal impairment may benefit from immunosuppressive therapy.

Intravenous urogram (IVU)
Intravenous urogram (IVU) is incorrect. Intravenous urogram (IVU) is useful for diagnosis of renal stones and ureteric tumours causing obstruction. Although renal stones may present with haematuria, there is typically no significant proteinuria.

Isotope renogram
Isotope renogram is incorrect. Isotope renogram would be useful to identify perfusion abnormalities in diagnosing renal artery stenosis. There is no suggestion of renal artery stenosis in this case and we would not be suspecting any perfusion abnormality.

Renal angiogram
Renal angiogram is incorrect. Renal angiogram would be used to assess the perfusion by renal arteries to the kidneys. This would be abnormal in renal artery stenosis and emboli. In patients with renal artery stenosis we would expect vastly unequal-sized kidneys, rather than the small discrepancy here.

Retrograde pyelogram
Retrograde pyelogram is incorrect. Retrograde pyelogram would be used to assess filling defects caused by stones or tumours, to help in placement of ureteral stents and preoperative assessment to delineate renal anatomy. It involves injection of a contrast into the ureter to visualise the ureters and kidneys. It is termed retrograde because the contrast flows in the opposite direction to the usual flow of urine. There is no suggestion of urinary obstruction in this case; therefore, this investigation is unhelpful.

stem: A 59-year-old man has sustained damage to the hypothalamus after a road traffic accident and period of hypotension associated with blood loss. He is suffering from hyperphagia. Which of the following structures is most likely to have been damaged?
explanation:
Ventromedial nucleus
The ventromedial nucleus is associated with regulation of satiety, the arcuate nucleus is another area of the hypothalamus involved in regulating feeding behaviour.

Dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus
Dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus is incorrect. This area of the hypothalamus is associated with control of blood pressure and heart rate.

Mammillary bodies
Mammillary bodies is incorrect. The mammillary bodies are involved in memory function.

Posterior nucleus
Posterior nucleus is incorrect. The posterior nucleus is involved in blood pressure regulation, the shivering response, and release of vasopressin.

Supraoptic nucleus
Supraoptic nucleus is incorrect. The supraoptic nucleus is involved in the control of release of vasopressin and oxytocin.

stem: A patient who had a myocardial infarction 6 months ago presents with firm, minutely lobulated enlargement of his gums. This is not associated with pain. On examination, it is most pronounced in the maxillary and mandibular anterior regions. He is diagnosed as having drug induced gingival hypertrophy. Which drug is most likely to be responsible for this?
explanation:
Amlodipine
Drug-induced gingival hypertrophy is a known side effect of Amlodipine. Gingival hypertrophy can occur as a side effect of the systemic medications listed below: Calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine, verapamil, diltiazem, oxodipine, amlodipine), a group of antihypertensive drugs Phenytoin, a drug used for the management of epilepsy, and other anticonvulsants such as sodium valproate, phenobarbital, and vigabatrin Ciclosporin, an immunosuppressant drug used to reduce organ transplant rejection Antibiotics such as erythromycin Hormones

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin is incorrect. Atorvastatin is not associated with drug-induced gingival hypertrophy. The side effects of statins include myalgia, myophathy, myositis and rhabdomyolysis. Statins can cause deranged liver function tests and rarely cause hepatits, jaundice, and pancreatitis. Other side effects include gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances, sleep disturbance, headache dizziness, paraaesthesia, peripheral neuropathy, fatigue, alopecia and hypersensitivity.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide mononitrate is incorrect. Isosorbide mononitrate is not known to cause gingival hypertrophy. The most common side effects include headache, hypotension, dizziness, drowsiness, weakness, and tachycardia. Rarely it can also cause hypersensitivity reactions.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin does not cause gingival hypertrophy. Common side effects of aspirin include diarrhoea, constipation, nausea, heartburn, and increased bruising. More serious side effects include gastrointestinal bleeding, tinnitus or loss of hearing, and hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol’s side effects does not include gum hypertrophy. The common side effects accosiated with beta blockers include blurred vision, cold hands/feet, confusion, difficulty breathing/shortness of breath/wheeze, dizziness, lightheadedness and tightness of the chest.

stem: You are examining the potential for a new thiazide diuretic that is not thought to increase renal potassium loss. Which one of the following accounts for the increased risk of hypokalaemia with bendroflumethiazide?
options: Increased delivery of sodium to the proximal convoluted tubule
Increased delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule
Increased delivery of potassium to the loop of Henle
Increased free water within the loop of Henle
Increased potassium excretion in the proximal convoluted tubule
explanation:
Increased delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule
Thiazide diuretics increase sodium loss into the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule, leading to: Increased activation of the aldosterone-sensitive sodium pump Thus, increased sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions Therefore causing hypokalaemic alkalosis Whilst they have less of an effect on increasing sodium excretion compared with loop diuretics, their effect on renal prostaglandins means that they are very effective antihypertensive agents.

Increased delivery of sodium to the proximal convoluted tubule
Increased delivery of sodium to the proximal convoluted tubule is incorrect. Thiazides do not increase delivery of sodium to the proximal convoluted tubule. Their mechanism of action is at the distal convoluted tubule where sodium-chloride symporter is inhibited. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors influence the proximal convoluted tubule.

Increased delivery of potassium to the loop of Henle
Increased delivery of potassium to the loop of Henle is incorrect. Thiazides cause sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium loss in the distal loop. Thiazides have no effect on the delivery of potassium to the loop of Henle.

Increased free water within the loop of Henle
Increased free water within the loop of Henle is incorrect. The mode of action of thiazides is at the distal convoluted tubule, not at the Loop of Henle which is more proximal. Loop diuretics such as furosemide act on the Na +-K +-2Cl − symporter) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle to inhibit sodium, chloride and potassium reabsorption.

Increased potassium excretion in the proximal convoluted tubule
Increased potassium excretion in the proximal convoluted tubule is incorrect. The increased potassium excretion occurs at the distal convoluted tubule. Acetazolamide and other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors acts at the proximal tubule to increase potassium excretion.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of abrupt collapse with loss of consciousness for approx 3 minutes. There is no subsequent confusion. She was noted to be pale during the episode. On examination, she had a mild tachycardia but the pulse was regular. Auscultation revealed normal first and second heart sounds and there were no audible murmurs. Neurological examination was normal. Routine bloods including complete blood count and random blood sugar were within normal range. ECG showed a sinus rhythm with no abnormalities noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vasovagal syncope
Vasovagal syncope is the most likely diagnosis here. Attacks of syncope may be exacerbated by breath holding or by paroxysms of coughing that obstruct venous return to the heart. Further there is no postictal confusion or lethargy or headache. Thus, in keeping with the history this is suggestive of a vasovagal syncope.

Atonic seizure
Atonic seizures is incorrect. Atonic seizures are typically drop attacks, which last seconds. The spectrum varies from head drop to complete loss of tone in the entire body.

Cardiogenic syncope
Cardiogenic syncope is incorrect. The patient is young and there is no history of arrhythmia, so cardiogenic syncope is also unlikely. Patients with a history of recurrent syncope are usually screened with 24-hour Holter monitoring to rule out cardiac arrhythmia.

Focal impaired awareness seizure
Focal impaired awareness seizure is incorrect. Loss of consciousness for less than 5 minutes and orientation post attack together suggest that these attacks are not epileptiform in nature. These types of seizure (previously termed complex partial seizure) is a type of focal seizure associated with a loss of consciousness. It usually begins with an aura (focal aware seizure) followed by involuntary complex motor activity during impaired consciousness like gum chewing, nose wiping, lip smacking. These seizures may evolve into secondarily generalised seizures. There may be postictal confusion. A 75 kg man develops adrenal insufficiency after a road traffic accident in which he suffered a significant period of hypotension. His corticosteroid needs are reviewed by the discharge team who need to determine what dose of prednisolone corresponds to physiological corticosteroid replacement. Which of the following prednisolone doses matches most closely with the physiological glucocorticoid production of a 75 kg man?

Pseudoseizure
Pseudoseizure is incorrect. Pseudoseizure is unlikely as the semiology is different. Pseudoseizures tend to have vigorous thrusting of shoulder and hip girdle and trunk as opposed to limb movements.

stem: A 75 kg man develops adrenal insufficiency after a road traffic accident in which he suffered a significant period of hypotension. His corticosteroid needs are reviewed by the discharge team who need to determine what dose of prednisolone corresponds to physiological corticosteroid replacement. Which of the following prednisolone doses matches most closely with the physiological glucocorticoid production of a 75 kg man?
explanation:
7.5 mg
This is a pure knowledge-based question, uncommon but not unheard of in the MRCP. 7.5 mg is said to equilibrate to the corticosteroid needs of an average 75 kg man. It should be noted that evening doses, long acting preparations (e.g. dexamethasone) and enzyme inhibitors increase the risk of adrenal suppression.

1 mg
1 mg is incorrect. This is an under dosage for the average basal requirement for this patient.

2.5 mg
2.5 mg is incorrect. This would under dose a 75 kg male and therefore would not meet his physiological corticosteroid requirement.

15 mg
15 mg is incorrect. However it is important to note that stressors will affect the dose requirement. In moderate intercurrent illness the dose should be doubled and therefore would be 15 mg in this patient.

20 mg
20 mg is incorrect. This would overdose an average basal requirement. Approximately 4 times the prednisolone dose in mg is said to be the equivalent dose when using hydrocortisone.

stem: Which of the following contains the highest amount of energy per gram?
explanation:
Triglycerides
Triglycerides are a type of fat (and the main constituents of body fat), and therefore have the highest content of calories. The guideline daily amount for consumption of fats in the UK diet is set at 70 g (20 g of saturated fat).

Muscle protein
Muscle protein is incorrect. Fats contain approximately 9 calories per gram, whereas carbohydrates and proteins contain 4 calories per gram of material.

Low-density lipoprotein
Low density lipoprotein is incorrect. Low-density lipoprotein contains both protein and lipids, and therefore per gram it contains less energy versus triglycerides alone.

Glucose
Glucose is incorrect. Fats have a higher energy content compared to carbohydrates like glucose. Nutritional Assessment, Malabsorption and Feeding

Starch
Starch is incorrect. Fats have a higher energy content compared to carbohydrates like starch.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a collapse. On further questioning she admits to problems with fainting over the past few years and her sodium is at the lower end of the normal range. Cortisol is below the lower limit of normal and you wonder about an inherited defect in cortisol production and plan to measure metabolic precursors to cortisol. What is the immediate precursor in the production of cortisol?
explanation:
11-Deoxycortisol
It is important to have at least a basic idea of pathways for steroid hormone synthesis, as a number of singlegene disorders are recognised to impact on hormone production. 11-Deoxycortisol is the direct precursor to cortisol.

Deoxycorticosterone
Chatin with AI is Tutor Deoxycorticosterone is incorrect. Deoxycorticosterone is the precursor for corticosterone, which turn the precursor for aldosterone.

17-Alpha hydroxyprogesterone
17-Alpha hydroxyprogesterone is incorrect. 17-Alpha hydroxyprogesterone forms an earlier step in the steroid synthesis pathway, and may act as a precursor for sex steroids, mineralocorticoids or corticosteroids.

Corticosterone
Corticosterone is incorrect. Corticosterone is the precursor step in the formation of aldosterone.

17-Alpha hydroxypregnenolone
17-alpha hydroxypregnenolone is incorrect. Similar to 17-alpha hydroxyprogesterone, 17-alpha hydroxypregnenolone also forms part of the steroid synthesis pathway and may also be a precursor for sex steroids, mineralocorticoids or corticosteroids.

stem: In which channel is the defect most likely to be found?
explanation:
Potassium
The most likely underlying diagnosis is congenital long QT syndrome. In this case the mode of inheritance is most likely to be autosomal dominant, although sporadic and recessive forms are also described. A number of defects in the potassium, calcium and sodium channels have been described, although genetic mutations leading to potassium channel defects are the most common. Beta-blockers are the initial therapy of choice, which prevent further episodes of VT in approximately 70% by reducing sympathetic outflow. In those who fail to respond, stellate ganglionectomy is an option and there is potential for implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) implantation. In those who have suffered a cardiac arrest, ICD implantation may be considered the initial therapy of choice.

Calcium
Calcium channel is incorrect. Mutations in calcium channels have been described to cause congenital long QT syndrome, but are much rarer than those in potassium channels.

Chloride
Chloride channel is incorrect. Problems with chloride channels are no thought to be linked to congenital long QT syndrome.

Magnesium
Magnesium channel is incorrect. Magnesium channels are no thought to be linked to congenital long QT syndrome. However, low levels of magnesium that may occur from starvation have the potential to lead to acquired long QT syndrome.

Sodium
Sodium channel is incorrect. Mutations in sodium channels have also been described as causing congenital long QT syndrome, but are much rarer than those in potassium channels.

stem: You are examining the prognostic significance of raised brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) in the management of heart failure. Where is BNP primarily produced in heart failure?
explanation:
Cardiac ventricles
Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a natriuretic hormone identified first in the brain but released primarily from the heart, particularly the ventricles. BNP is thought to be produced in response to ventricular stretch, which occurs as a result of sodium and water overload.

Aortic arch
Aortic arch is incorrect. The aortic arch contains the aortic bodies, a cluster of peripheral chemoreceptors and baroreceptors. These detect changes in blood pressure and arterial blood composition and are responsible for feeding back into the brain in order to regulate breathing and blood pressure.

Carotid body
Carotid body is incorrect. Carotid bodies are chemoreceptors that lie near the bifurcation of the carotid artery. Similar to aortic bodies, they detect changes in the composition of arterial blood (such as partial pressure of oxygen and carbon dioxide, and changes in pH) and help in the regulation of breathing.

Hypothalamus
Hypothalamus is incorrect. The hypothalamus secretes neurohormones (thyrotropin-releasing hormone, corticotropin-releasing hormone, dopamine, growth hormone-releasing hormone, gonadotropin-releasing hormone and somatostatin) which in turn regulate the production of pituitary hormones

Cardiac atria
Cardiac atria is incorrect. The atria are responsible for producing atrial natriuretic peptide, a natriuretic hormone similar to BNP but with a higher affinity for the receptors to which it binds and a half-life that is half as long.

stem: A healthy and generally active 28-year-old woman performs her daily 5-mile run. Which one of the following physiological parameters is most likely to increase as she performs this exercise?
explanation:
Stroke volume
During exercise, the body must increase blood flow and hence oxygen delivery to the coronary circulation and skeletal muscle, where oxygen utilisation is greatest. This is done in a number of ways. Dilatation of the blood vessels within the exercising muscles causes a fall in total peripheral resistance, resulting in a decrease in diastolic blood pressure. This decrease in venous compliance (dilatation), caused by sympathetic stimulation, helps to maintain ventricular filling during diastole. The pulmonary vessels undergo passive dilatation as more blood flows into the pulmonary circulation, decreasing pulmonary vascular resistance. Increased venous return to the heart results in an increase in stroke volume. Multiple stimuli, including increased oxygen consumption, stimulate increased heart rate. Both increased heart rate and stroke volume increase cardiac output. Systemic arterial pressure also increases in response to the increase in cardiac output.

Diastolic pressure
Diastolic pressure is incorrect. Diastolic pressure is decreased as a result of dilatation of the blood vessels within the exercising muscles leading to a fall in peripheral resistance.

Peripheral vascular resistance
Peripheral vascular resistance is incorrect. Peripheral resistance falls due to dilatation of the blood vessels in the exercising muscles.

Pulmonary vascular resistance
Pulmonary vascular resistance is incorrect. Pulmonary vascular resistance decreases due to passive dilatation of the pulmonary vessels allowing for more blood to flow into the pulmonary circulation. A healthy medical student performs a series of pulmonary investigations as part of the respiratory physiology lab. Which one of the following is higher at the apex of the lung than at the base when he is standing?

Venous compliance
Venous compliance is incorrect. Venous compliance is decreased by sympathetic stimulation.

stem: A healthy medical student performs a series of pulmonary investigations as part of the respiratory physiology lab. Which one of the following is higher at the apex of the lung than at the base when he is standing?
explanation:
V/Q ratio
Regional variations in lung physiology are classically attributed to gravity; however, structural variation in airways and blood vessels is also likely to play a role. The apex is situated above the level of the heart, therefore a greater volume of blood will preferentially flow to the base than upstream to the apex. The alveoli at the base are compressed by the weight of the lungs and thus are smaller than those at the apex. Compliance is volume change per unit pressure change; as they start at a smaller volume, basal alveoli demonstrate greater compliance than apical alveoli. The reduced compliance means that less inspired gas goes to the apex than to the base; i.e. ventilation is reduced at the apex. Less blood flow and less ventilation occurs at the apex; however, the reduction in ventilation is less than the reduction in blood flow so the V/Q ratio at the top of the lung is greater than it is at the bottom. The increased V/Q ratio at the apex makes PaCO 2 lower and PaO 2 higher at the apex than they are at the base.

Blood flow
Blood flow is incorrect. The apex is situated above the level of the heart, therefore a greater volume of blood will preferentially flow to the base than upstream to the apex.

Compliance
Compliance is incorrect. The alveoli at the base are compressed by the weight of the lungs and thus smaller than those at the apex. Compliance is volume change per unit pressure change; as they start at a smaller volume, basal alveoli demonstrate greater compliance than apical.

PaCO 2
PaCO 2 is incorrect. The increased V/Q ratio at the apex makes PaCO 2 lower and PaO 2 higher at the apex than they are at the base.

Ventilation
Ventilation is incorrect. Basal alveoli demonstrate greater compliance than apical alveoli. The reduced compliance means that less inspired gas goes to the apex than to the base; ie ventilation is reduced at the apex.

stem: A 54-year-old male is brought to his GP by his wife. She states that his facial features have changed, describing coarsening. On direct questioning he admits to an increasing shoe size and being no longer able to wear his wedding ring. After appropriate investigations a growth hormone-secreting adenoma is found. In health, the secretion of growth hormone is increased by which one of the following?
explanation:
Exercise
Growth hormone (GH) is synthesised, stored and secreted by the endocrine cells of the anterior pituitary. Its release is stimulated by growth hormone-releasing hormone and inhibited by somatostatin. Numerous factors serve as a stimulus for GH release, including: 1. moderate to severe exercise 2. hypoglycaemia (eg insulin administration) 3. stress due to emotional disturbances, illness and fever. In contrast, a number of factors inhibit growth hormone release, including: 1. free fatty acids 2. hyperglycaemia 3. growth hormone itself (negative feedback).

Free fatty acids
Free fatty acids is incorrect. Free fatty acids inhibit growth hormone release.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. Growth hormone release is stimulated by growth hormone-releasing hormone. Growth hormone acts by negative feedback to inhibit growth hormone release.

Hyperglycaemia
Hyperglycaemia is incorrect. Hypoglycaemia acts as a stimulus for growth hormone release. 6 A 65-year-old smoker with a history of transient ischaemic attacks presents with loss of co-ordination of his right side. On examination there is decreased skin sensation in the right half of his face and the left half of his body. In addition he has a right Horner syndrome. Which vessel is most likely to be involved?

Somatostatin
Somatostatin is incorrect. Growth hormone release is inhibited by somatostatin.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker with a history of transient ischaemic attacks presents with loss of co-ordination of his right side. On examination there is decreased skin sensation in the right half of his face and the left half of his body. In addition he has a right Horner syndrome. Which vessel is most likely to be involved?
explanation:
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Involvement of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery is called Wallenberg syndrome, with ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia caused by infarction of the inferior part of the cerebellum. A combination of additional deficits is attributed to infarction of the dorsolateral medulla: 1. decreased skin sensation in the ipsilateral half of the face and the contralateral half of the body 2. ipsilateral Horner syndrome 3. ipsilateral weakness of the soft palate, larynx and pharynx 4. rotatory vertigo. This syndrome is distinct from other territory infarctions.

Basilar artery
Basilar artery is incorrect. Basilar artery: motor and bulbar symptoms associated with altered conscious state. Visual and balance symptoms also possible.

Internal carotid artery
Internal carotid artery is incorrect. Internal carotid artery: may be silent, through to devastating stroke and death. ICA classical features include transient monocular blindness and haemodynamically variable symptoms (i.e. orthostatically provoked ischaemic symptoms).

Middle cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery is incorrect. Middle cerebral artery: largest and most commonly affected. Contralateral hemiplegia, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia.

Posterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Posterior cerebral artery: less common than anterior circulation strokes. Diverse spectrum of symptoms including visual loss, dizziness, headache, confusion and nausea in addition to more classical weakness.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted to hospital with persistent vomiting. A background of fatigue is elicited. He is clinically dehydrated and hypotensive. His serum sodium concentration is 124 mmol/l, potassium 4.9 mmol/l, urea 9.8 mmol/l, creatinine 96 μmol/l. Urine sodium concentration in a specimen passed on admission is 62 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the hyponatraemia?
explanation:
Adrenal failure
This patient is dehydrated, with profound hyponatraemia and evidence of renal sodium wasting (natriuresis) inappropriate in a patient who should be attempting to conserve sodium and thus water. Natriuresis in a dehydrated, hyponatraemic patient suggests that there is uncontrolled renal loss of sodium. This is classically seen in adrenal failure. The vomiting, fatigue and hypotension are also consistent with adrenal failure.

Cerebral salt wasting
Cerebral salt wasting is incorrect. Cerebral salt wasting can also cause dehydration and hyponatraemia owing to excessive natriuresis. There is no indication, however, of neurological disease, trauma or surgery, making this less likely in this patient.

Gastrointestinal fluid loss
Gastrointestinal fluid loss is incorrect. Hyponatraemia and dehydration due to gastrointestinal fluid loss should lead to renal conservation of sodium, not the natriuresis seen here.

Low sodium intake
Low sodium intake is incorrect. Sodium deficiency due to a low intake should lead to renal conservation of sodium, not the natriuresis seen here.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is incorrect. Although SIADH is an important cause of hyponatraemia and sodium excretion may be high, the hyponatraemia is due to water excess and patients are not dehydrated.

stem: Some 24 h after sustaining severe skeletal and soft tissue trauma in a road traffic collision, a 19-year-old man becomes oliguric. Which one of the following would be least likely to present if acute tubular necrosis (ATN) were the diagnosis?
options: Urinary sodium concentration less than 10 mmol/l
explanation:
Urinary sodium concentration less than 10 mmol/l
The question is asking which of these findings makes ATN the LEAST likely diagnosis. Urine osmolality <250 can be seen in ATN but is not specific for ATN. A urine sodium <10 strongly suggests that renal tubular function is intact and that the issue is pre-renal, hence why it is the correct answer here. Trauma can cause oliguria via a number of mechanisms. 1. A stress-induced rise in blood glucose concentration can cause glycosuria, regardless of renal function. 2. Tissue breakdown and decreased urine production can cause both hyperkalaemia and hyperuricaemia, again regardless of renal function. 3. A low urine osmolality (< 250 mmol/kg) is possible in ATN; however, it is very non-specific; it can also be seen in pre-renal causes of oliguria. 4. A urinary sodium concentration less than 10 mmol/l strongly suggests that renal tubular function is intact, making this the correct answer. If oliguria were prerenal, it would be expected that the urine would be concentrated as a result of hypovolaemic stimulation of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) secretion.

Glycosuria
Glycosuria is incorrect. A stress-induced rise in blood glucose concentration can cause glycosuria, regardless of renal function.

Hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia is incorrect. Tissue breakdown and decreased urine production can cause hyperkalaemia regardless of renal function.

Hyperuricaemia
Hyperuricaemia is incorrect. Tissue breakdown and decreased urine production can cause hyperuricaemia, regardless of renal function.

Urinary osmolality less than 250 mmol/kg
Urinary osmolality less than 250 mmol/kg is incorrect. A low urine osmolality (< 250 mmol/kg) is possible in ATN, however, it is very non-specific; it can also be seen in pre-renal causes of oliguria.

stem: A 77-year-old man presents with a history of vomiting undigested food. Routine biochemistry shows a serum bicarbonate concentration of 38 mmol/l. Which one of the following findings would most strongly suggest that he had a chronic metabolic alkalosis?
explanation:
Elevated arterial pCO2
The development of hypercapnia as compensation for metabolic alkalosis does tend to take some time, implying chronicity. Although alkalosis inhibits respiration, rising pCO 2 acts as a respiratory stimulant. It takes time for the sensitivity of the respiratory centre to decline, allowing sustained elevated arterial pCO 2.

Alkaline urine
Alkaline urine is incorrect. In prolonged metabolic alkalosis, the urine may become acidic, reflecting increased proximal bicarbonate resorption (due to hypochloraemia).

Base excess 18 mmol/l
Base excess 18 mmol/l is incorrect. The base excess provides no additional information about this patient: it is directly related to the high bicarbonate concentration of 38 mmol/l.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. Gastric secretions contain about 10 mmol/l potassium and, although potassium depletion is likely to become more severe the longer vomiting occurs, hypokalaemia can develop at any time.

Hypomagnesaemia
Hypomagnesaemia is incorrect. Hypomagnesaemia is frequently found in patients with potassium depletion.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with vomiting, nausea and anorexia, which has been progressive over the past few weeks. He has a serum creatinine concentration of 522 μmol/l. Which one of the following features, if present, would help most to identify possible aetiologies for his kidney disease and suggest that it is longstanding?
explanation:
Small kidneys on ultrasound examination
Anaemia certainly implies a degree of chronicity to the kidney disease (due to decreased erythropoietin secretion) but sheds no light on its possible cause. The same is true of secondary hyperparathyroidism (due to decreased calcitriol secretion and hypocalcaemia). Similarly, hyperuricaemia is common in chronic kidney disease of any aetiology due to reduced excretion. Hypotension can cause acute kidney disease (which untreated may progress to chronic). However, it can also be a consequence of kidney disease. Renal size is therefore the most useful for delineating aetiology and chronicity. The kidneys are usually decreased in size in chronic kidney disease, except when this is a result of amyloid or polycystic disease, in which case they are enlarged. Kidneys are usually normal in size in advanced diabetic nephropathy. Affected kidneys are initially enlarged in the acute phase from hyperfiltration.

Anaemia
Anaemia is incorrect. Although anaemia implies a degree of chronicity to the kidney disease it does not give any indication of its possible cause.

High serum parathyroid hormone concentration
High serum parathyroid hormone concentration is incorrect. Decreased calcitrol secretion and hypocalcaemia result in secondary hyperparathyroidism, but do not give any indication of its possible cause.

Hyperuricaemia
Hyperuricaemia is incorrect. Hyperuricaemia is common in chronic kidney disease of any aetiology as a result of reduced excretion but does not give any indication of its possible cause.

Hypotension
Hypotension is incorrect. Hypotension can cause acute kidney disease, which can then become chronic if left untreated, but hypotension can also be a consequence of kidney disease, and would not give any indication of its possible cause.

stem: A 71-year-old man with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe shortness of breath. Blood gas analysis shows: arterial [H +] 55 nmol/l (pH 7.26), pCO 2 9.4 kPa, pO 2 9.1 kPa, derived [HCO 3–] 33 mmol/l. Which one of the following types of acid–base disturbance is most likely?
options: Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
explanation:
Exacerbation of chronic respiratory acidosis
The patient is acidotic. The high pCO2 indicates a respiratory acidosis. Were this to be acute, the bicarbonate concentration would be normal or only marginally elevated and a higher hydrogen ion concentration would be expected – hence there is a chronic respiratory acidosis. Hydrogen ion concentration increases by approximately 5.5 nmol/l for each increase in pCO 2 by 1 kPa in an acute disturbance. The raised bicarbonate implies a degree of compensation and hence chronicity. Were compensation to be complete, the patient would be expected to be less acidotic with a higher bicarbonate concentration, thus there is a degree of acute exacerbation. The data are compatible with both an acute exacerbation of a chronic respiratory acidosis and a mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis, but the clinical setting makes the former the more likely. The elevated bicarbonate concentration is incompatible with a metabolic acidosis.

Acute respiratory acidosis
Acute respiratory acidosis is incorrect. For this to be an acute respiratory acidosis the bicarbonate would be expected to be normal or only marginally elevated, and the hydrogen ion concentration would be expected to be higher.

Chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis
Chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis is incorrect. For this to be a chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis the expectation would be for the patient to be less acidotic with a higher bicarbonate concentration. The results here indicate a degree of acute exacerbation.

Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis is incorrect. Although the data are compatible with mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis the clinical setting in the scenario makes acute exacerbation of chronic respiratory acidosis much more likely.

Severe metabolic acidosis
Severe metabolic acidosis is incorrect. The elevated bicarbonate concentration is not compatible with a metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman on nasogastric aspiration for paralytic ileus following surgery develops a metabolic alkalosis. Which one of the following intravenous fluids would be the preferred treatment for the alkalosis?
explanation:
Normal (0.9%) saline
The metabolic alkalosis, being secondary to a loss of gastric contents and hence acid, is a hypochloraemic alkalosis. 1. There is predominant loss of H + and chloride ions. 2. The alkalosis is perpetuated by the hypochloraemia, which prevents renal excretion of the excess bicarbonate since its proximal tubular reabsorption (with sodium) is enhanced.

5% dextrose
5% dextrose is incorrect. The treatment here is to provide adequate chloride ions to allow excess bicarbonate to be excreted, correcting the alkalosis. Dextrose 5% contains no chloride.

Dextrose saline
Dextrose saline is incorrect. The treatment here is to provide adequate chloride ions to allow excess bicarbonate to be excreted, correcting the acidosis; dextrose saline contains insufficient chloride for this purpose.

Ringer's lactate
Ringer’s lactate is incorrect. The treatment here is to provide adequate chloride ions to allow excess bicarbonate to be excreted, correcting the acidosis. Ringer’s lactate is inappropriate as metabolism to bicarbonate of the lactate it contains would exacerbate the alkalosis.

Twice normal (1.8%) saline
Twice normal saline (1.8%) is incorrect. The treatment here is to provide adequate chloride ions to allow excess bicarbonate to be excreted, correcting the acidosis. Although twice normal saline is occasionally used for treatment of severe hyponatraemia, it has no place in this clinical situation.

stem: A 21-year-old man takes advantage of his employer’s health benefits and undergoes a private health screen. Urinalysis is positive for protein on two occasions, once at the health screen and a later repeated sample at the GP. His serum urea and creatinine concentrations are normal. Which one of the following would be the most important investigations to perform next?
options: Measurement of urine protein immediately on getting out of bed in the morning
Mid-stream urine for culture and sensitivity
explanation:
Measurement of urine protein immediately on getting out of bed in the morning
Proteinuria can occur because of: glomerular damage tubular damage (hence the decreased reabsorption of the small amount of low-molecular-weight proteins that are normally filtered by the glomeruli) an increased concentration of low-molecular-weight proteins in the blood (e.g. immunoglobulin light chains in myeloma – Bence Jones protein) secretion of proteins into the urine (e.g. in urinary tract infection) orthostatic proteinuria; a benign condition where protein is present in the urine when an individual is upright, but not when they have been supine for a period. In a young, otherwise well person orthostatic proteinuria should be ruled out before more extensive investigations are carried out.

24-hour urine protein excretion
24-hour urine protein excretion is incorrect. 24-hour urine protein quantifies severity but is of limited use in determining cause.

Creatinine clearance
Creatinine clearance is incorrect. Creatinine clearance is likely to be normal in this young, well patient with normal urea and creatinine; it would, however, form part of subsequent investigations.

Mid-stream urine for culture and sensitivity
Mid-stream urine for culture and sensitivity is incorrect. M, C & S is unlikely to reveal acute infection after two separate proteinuria results.

Urine protein electrophoresis
Urine protein electrophoresis is incorrect. Tubular proteins and Bence Jones protein can be detected by electrophoresis of concentrated urine if the more benign orthostatic proteinuria is excluded.

stem: A 32-year-old man is referred to a dermatologist with soft, fleshy lumps over his elbows. Examination also reveals that he has yellow fat deposits in his palmar creases. His (fasting) serum cholesterol concentration is 12.4 mmol/l, triglyceride 14.2 mmol/l. Which one of the following groups of lipoprotein particles is likely to be present in excess?
explanation:
Intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL)
The clinical description (i.e. soft, fleshy lumps over the elbows and yellow fat deposits in the palmar creases) and elevation of cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations to approximately equal levels is typical of familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia. This condition is also known as remnant dyslipidaemia, broad beta disease and type-III hyperlipidaemia. It is caused by an inherited abnormality of the remnant receptor responsible for the removal of intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) from the circulation by the liver. Elevated total cholesterol and triglyceride levels, IDL and VLDL remnant are typical. There is a significant risk for developing coronary artery disease. The presence of palmar xanthoma is considered pathognomonic for this disorder.

Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons is incorrect. Chylomicrons contain little cholesterol: they are the carriers of dietary lipids in the blood. Excesses of chylomicrons can manifest as xanthomas, but not of the type described here.

Lipoprotein (a)
Lipoprotein (a) is incorrect. Lipoprotein (a) is a modified form of LDL and appears to be an independent risk factor for coronary disease. Excesses of lipoprotein (a) can manifest as xanthomas, but not of the type described here.

Low-density lipoproteins (LDL)
Low-density lipoproteins (LDL) is incorrect. LDL are the principal carriers of cholesterol. Excesses of LDL can manifest as xanthomas, but not of the type described here.

High-density lipoproteins (HDL)
High-density lipoproteins (HDL) is incorrect. HDL excess is not associated with dysbetalipoprotenemias.

stem: A 21-year-old man is alarmed as he has suffered a significant decrease in his exercise tolerance and shortness of breath, a few days before he is to leave on a backpacking holiday in Southeast Asia. He consults his GP, who observes that he is slightly jaundiced and pale. Deficiency of which one of the following enzymes could best explain these clinical features?
explanation:
Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Deficiency of red cell glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase is a common inherited disorder, which renders red cells susceptible to increases in oxidative stress. Antimalarial drugs are among several that can cause haemolysis by increasing oxidative stress in such patients and potentially explain the presentation here Many different mutations in the enzyme have been described, and the range of clinical severity is wide

Bilirubin glucuronyl transferase
Bilirubin glucuronyl transferase is incorrect. Decreased bilirubin glucuronyl transferase activity causes an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Disorders include Gilbert syndrome and Crigler–Najjar disease. As the excess bilirubin is unconjugated, it does not appear in the urine.

Glucose 6-phosphatase
Glucose 6-phosphatase is incorrect. Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase causes type-1 glycogen storage disease.

Hydroxymethylbilane synthase
Hydroxymethylbilane synthase is incorrect. Hydroxymethylbilane synthase (or porphobilinogen deaminase) deficiency is the cause of acute intermittent porphyria. Some antimalarials may precipitate attacks, urine darkens on standing during attacks; however, there is no jaundice.

Pyruvate kinase
Pyruvate kinase is incorrect. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a rare cause of haemolytic anaemia. Haemoglobinuria would cause darkening of the urine. This deficiency, however, is much less common than glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

stem: A 25-year-old man, previously rather sedentary in his habits but alarmed by his increasing weight, is persuaded by his girlfriend to join a gym, and begins an exercise programme. Although there are several similar people enrolled in the programme, he finds that he is unable to keep up with them because of muscle pain, particularly in his legs. Within a few minutes of resting, however, the pains resolve. Investigation revealed a slight fall in blood lactate concentration during exercise. Which one of the following is most likely to be the cause of his complaint?
explanation:
Decreased muscle glycogenolysis
In intense activity working muscle is more dependent on breakdown of muscle glycogen than uptake from the bloodstream. Decreased muscle glycogenolysis classically causes muscle pain on exercise resolving on rest in McArdle disease. McArdle disease is an inherited deficiency of muscle phosphorylase. This prevents adequate muscle glycogenolysis, apparent at times of increased muscular activity.

Decreased hepatic glycogenolysis
Decreased hepatic glycogenolysis is incorrect. Decreased hepatic glycogenolysis would not cause local muscle pain.

Decreased muscle glucose uptake
Decreased muscle glucose uptake is incorrect. In intense activity working muscle is more dependent on breakdown of muscle glycogen than uptake from the bloodstream.

Impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis
Impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis is incorrect. Impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis would not cause local muscle pain. 8

Premature atherosclerosis
Premature atherosclerosis is incorrect. An ischaemic cause for muscle pain induced by exercise is excluded by a failure of lactate concentration to rise during exercise.

stem: A 75-year-old woman undergoes total gastrectomy for carcinoma of the stomach. With which one of the following nutrients is she most likely to require parenteral replacement?
explanation:
Vitamin B12
No significant absorption of nutrients takes place in the stomach. The absorption of vitamin B 12 1. takes place in the terminal ileum 2. is critically dependent on the availability of intrinsic factor 3. intrinsic factor is only secreted by the parietal (oxyntic) cells of the stomach; hence, patients who have had a total gastrectomy require parenteral replacement of vitamin B 12. The remaining nutrients listed above are absorbed in bowel without any gastric factors. Regardless, patients who have had total gastrectomies may require general nutritional supplementation (e.g. high-energy, high-protein drinks) due to: 1. lack of pepsin secretion 2. reduced activation of pancreatic proenzymes 3. a greatly reduced ability to eat normal amounts of food.

Ascorbic acid
Ascorbic acid is incorrect. Ascorbic acid is absorbed in the bowel without any gastric factors.

Folic acid
Folic acid is incorrect. Folic acid is absorbed in the bowel without any gastric factors.

Iron
Iron is incorrect. Iron is absorbed in the bowel without any gastric factors.

Vitamin D
Vitamin D is incorrect. Vitamin D is absorbed in the bowel without any gastric factors.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain and drowsiness. She is noted to have frequent, deep, sighing respirations. ABG analysis reveals: pH 6.9 pO 2 12.4 kPa pCO 2 2.48 kPa HCO 3 - 4.7 mmol/l Base excess -29.8 mmol/l In this clinical context of metabolic acidosis, which of the following mediates the observed increased respiratory drive?
options: Central chemoreceptor response to CO 2 content of CSF
Central chemoreceptor response to O2 content of CSF
The aortic body located in the root of the aorta
The carotid bodies in the common carotid arteries
The decreased plasma CO2 causing central chemoreceptor stimulation of the inspiratory area of the
explanation:
The carotid bodies in the common carotid arteries
Ventilation is controlled by the respiratory centre in the medulla. This receives afferents from the peripheral and central chemoreceptors. The patient in diabetic ketoacidosis demonstrates an increased respiratory drive in response to metabolic acidosis. Plasma pH is sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid bodies and to a lesser extent in the aortic arch. Control of normal ventilation is by the central chemoreceptors, in response to plasma carbon dioxide tension. The central chemoreceptor sites are responsible for approximately two-thirds of the ventilatory response. Carbon dioxide freely diffuses across the blood-brain barrier into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), where it hydrates, then dissociates into H + ions.

Central chemoreceptor response to CO 2 content of CSF
Central chemoreceptor response to CO 2 content of CSF is incorrect. Decreased pH as sensed by the central chemoreceptors stimulates the respiratory centre to drive faster, deeper ventilation, lowering CO 2 . The central chemoreceptors do not directly sense CO 2 or H + ions.

Central chemoreceptor response to O2 content of CSF
Central chemoreceptor response to O 2 content of CSF is incorrect. Peripheral chemoreceptors also mediate the response to plasma oxygen tension and temperature.

The aortic body located in the root of the aorta
The aortic body located in the root of the aorta is incorrect. Plasma pH is sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid bodies and to a lesser extent in the aortic arch, not the root.

The decreased plasma CO2 causing central chemoreceptor stimulation of the inspiratory area of the
The decreased plasma CO2 causing central chemoreceptor stimulation of the inspiratory area of the brain The decreased plasma CO 2 causing central chemoreceptor stimulation of the inspiratory area of the brain is incorrect. Increased [H +] as sensed by the central chemoreceptors stimulates the respiratory centre to drive faster, deeper ventilation, lowering CO 2 towards normal.

stem: A 74-year-old male stops smoking after a 50-pack year smoking history. He sees his GP with a marked increase in coughing and sputum production. His GP, after initial assessment and investigations, reassures him that this reflects recovery of the function of his respiratory tract lining. Which of the following physiological characteristics relates to the lining of the respiratory tract?
options: Approximately 1 litre of mucus is produced each day
The bronchioles have cartilage in their wall
The bronchioles have diameters of up to 5 mm
The cilia are under the control of a physiological motor, dynein
The mucociliary escalator moves at 0.2 cm/min
explanation:
The cilia are under the control of a physiological motor, dynein
The mucociliary escalator has an essential role in clearing debris, including pathogens from the respiratory tract. Ciliary dynein converts chemical energy from ATP into movement, producing rhythmic ciliary beating. Cigarette smoke causes a secondary ciliary dyskinesia. Primary ciliary dyskinesia – Kartagener’s syndrome – is due to an absence of dynein.

Approximately 1 litre of mucus is produced each day
Approximately 1 litre of mucus is produced each day is incorrect. Approximately 100 ml of mucus is produced by the respiratory tract each day.

The bronchioles have cartilage in their wall
The bronchioles have cartilage in their wall is incorrect. Bronchi become bronchioles by definition when they no longer contain cartilage in their walls.

The bronchioles have diameters of up to 5 mm
The bronchioles have diameters of up to 5 mm is incorrect. Bronchi become bronchioles by definition when they no longer contain cartilage in their walls, usually when they are as narrow as 1 mm in diameter.

The mucociliary escalator moves at 0.2 cm/min
The mucociliary escalator moves at 0.2 cm/min is incorrect. In health, the mucociliary escalator moves at 2 cm/min.

stem: A 60-year-old male is given 22 ml of 10 mg/ml IV injection of a drug. The plasma concentration at equilibrium is 15 mg/l, urine concentration is 150 mg/l and he produces 1440 ml of urine during a 24-h collection. The drug is freely filtered at the glomerulus and is not actively secreted or absorbed by the kidney. What is the clearance of the substance?
options: Cannot say from the information given
explanation:
10 ml/min
The answer is 10 ml/min (Option C). Clearance is given by the formula (U × V)/P where: U = urine concentration in mg/ml V = urine volume produced in ml/min P = plasma concentration in mg/ml Care must be taken to ensure values entered into the calculation are in the correct units: U = 150 mg/l = 0.15 mg/ml V = 1440 ml/24 h = 1440 ml/1440 min = 1 ml/min P = 15 mg/l = 0.015 mg/ml Clearance therefore = (0.15 × 1)/0.015 = 10 ml/min

0.1 ml/min
0.1 ml/min (Option A) is incorrect. A common pitfall is a magnitude of 10 or 100 error, as units are not converted.

1 ml/min
1 ml/min (Option B) is incorrect. A common pitfall is a magnitude of 10 or 100 error, as units are not converted.

100 ml/min
100 ml/min (Option D) is incorrect. A common pitfall is a magnitude of 10 or 100 error, as units are not converted.

Cannot say from the information given
Cannot say from the information given (Option E) is incorrect. All the required information is given. Patient age/sex and bolus quantity/concentration are irrelevant to clearance.

stem: A 54-year-old male, with a suspected new diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), is sent for pulmonary function tests. During the tests he is required to inhale a small volume of carbon monoxide. He is told that this is to measure his diffusing capacity, or how well his lungs exchange gases. Which of the following physiological principles best describes pulmonary gas exchange?
options: Carbon dioxide is less water soluble than oxygen
Gas exchange can occur in the final seven branches of the bronchoalveolar tree
Only about 0.15% of oxygen is carried in solution in the plasma
The equilibration of gases takes about 2.5 s in the resting lung
The first 12 branches of the bronchial tree are collectively known as the conducting zone
explanation:
Gas exchange can occur in the final seven branches of the bronchoalveolar tree
On average the bronchi divide 23 times. The initial 16 branches or so are known as the conducting zone and do not take part in gas exchange. Generation 17–23 contain alveoli and take part in gas exchange.

Carbon dioxide is less water soluble than oxygen
Carbon dioxide is less water soluble than oxygen is incorrect. This is in part due to its low water solubility; much less than that of CO 2. 5–10% of CO 2 is carried dissolved in plasma.

Only about 0.15% of oxygen is carried in solution in the plasma
Only about 0.15% of oxygen is carried in solution in the plasma is incorrect. Only approximately 1.5% of oxygen is carried in solution in the plasma.

The equilibration of gases takes about 2.5 s in the resting lung
The equilibration of gases takes about 2.5 s in the resting lung is incorrect. The equilibration of gases takes about 0.25 s in the resting lung, decreasing in high cardiac output states as red cell transit time decreases.

The first 12 branches of the bronchial tree are collectively known as the conducting zone
The first 12 branches of the bronchial tree are collectively known as the conducting zone is incorrect. The initial 16 branches or so are known as the conducting zone.

stem: A 38-year-old woman, with a raised BMI, presents to the GP with symptoms of severe heartburn. Focused history revealed copious NSAID use, but no 'red flag' symptoms. No other medical or surgical history is available. Upper GI endoscopy revealed mucosal breaks extending between the tops of two mucosal folds, involving 60% of the mucosal circumference in the oesophagus. Manometry revealed a reduced mean lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure. Which of the following clinical conditions best fits these findings?
options: Grade D oesophagitis post-laparoscopic Nissen’s fundoplication
explanation:
Grade C oesophagitis
Reflux oesophagitis, or gastro-oesophageal reflex disease (GORD) refers to prolonged or excessive reflux of gastric contents with resulting inflammatory damage of the oesophagus. The Los Angeles system allows endoscopic grading of severity: 1. Grade A: one or more mucosal breaks < 5 mm, none of which extends between the tops of the mucosal folds 2. Grade B: one or more mucosal breaks > 5 mm, none of which extends between the tops of the mucosal folds 3. Grade C: mucosal breaks extending between the tops of mucosal folds, involving < 75% of the mucosal circumference 4. Grade D: mucosal breaks involving > 75% of the mucosal circumference. Grade C oesophagitis, whether or not associated with a hiatus hernia, has reduced mean lower oesophageal sphincter pressures.

Achalasia
Achalasia is incorrect. In achalasia, manometry will reveal high resting LOS pressure, failure of LOS relaxation with swallowing and lack of useful peristalsis. The net effect will be a raised mean LOS pressure.

Diffuse oesophageal spasm
Diffuse oesophageal spasm is incorrect. Diffuse oesophageal spasm will show an excessive proportion of simultaneous pressure waves in the presence of peristalsis, again increasing mean LOS pressure.

Grade D oesophagitis post-laparoscopic Nissen’s fundoplication
Grade D oesophagitis post-laparoscopic Nissen’s fundoplication is incorrect. Nissen’s fundoplication will restore LOS pressure above normal.

Nutcracker oesophagus
Nutcracker oesophagus is incorrect. Nutcracker oesophagus, also known as hypertensive peristalsis, will be associated with excessive amplitude contractions, and thus a raised mean LOS pressure.

stem: When taking a history from a 61-year-old woman with disseminated sclerosis, you ascertain that she is intermittently incontinent for liquid stools. Which one of the following pertains to the clinical physiology of faecal continence?
options: Anal ultrasound is widely used to assess sphincter function
Incontinence may be associated with rectal prolapse
Involuntary faecal continence is controlled by the external anal sphincter
The commonest cause of sphincter weakness is pudendal neuropathy
Voluntary faecal continence is controlled by the internal anal sphincter
explanation:
Incontinence may be associated with rectal prolapse
Around 50% of patients with rectal prolapse may have some degree of incontinence, this can be graded as incontinence to flatus, liquid stool or solid stool. Investigations Anal ultrasound is widely used to assess sphincter structure, not function. Anal manometry is used to assess function. Clinical history - Important points to elicit: ability to defer defecation by more than 15 min use of constipating medication regular usage of pads or anal plugs.

Anal ultrasound is widely used to assess sphincter function
Anal ultrasound is widely used to assess sphincter function is incorrect. Anal ultrasound is widely used to assess sphincter structure, not function. Anal manometry is used to assess function.

Involuntary faecal continence is controlled by the external anal sphincter
Involuntary faecal continence is controlled by the external anal sphincter is incorrect. Involuntary faecal continence is controlled by the internal anal sphincter.

The commonest cause of sphincter weakness is pudendal neuropathy
The commonest cause of sphincter weakness is pudendal neuropathy is incorrect as the most common cause of sphincter weakness is sphincter damage and atrophy, although pudendal neuropathy may contribute. Faecal incontinence may be associated with constipation, owing to overflow. A critically ill patient on the ICU shows evidence of impaired oxygen delivery to the tissues. The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left by which one of the following factors?

Voluntary faecal continence is controlled by the internal anal sphincter
Voluntary faecal continence is controlled by the internal anal sphincter is incorrect. Voluntary faecal continence is controlled by the external anal sphincter.

stem: A critically ill patient on the ICU shows evidence of impaired oxygen delivery to the tissues. The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left by which one of the following factors?
explanation:
Rise in pH
A rise in pH shifts the dissociation curve to the left, increasing oxygen affinity and impairing oxygen offloading in the tissues. The following shift the dissociation curve to the right, decreasing oxygen affinity (and aiding oxygen offloading in the tissues): rise in 2,3-DPG (2,3-diphosphoglycerate) rise in plasma temperature rise in blood CO 2 content fall in plasma bicarbonate concentration.

Fall in plasma bicarbonate concentration
Functional residual capacity of 3.5 litres Functional residual capacity of 3.5 litres is incorrect. Although it is closer to physiological, it is too large to be likely in comparison to the correct answer, which is spot on.

Rise in blood CO2 content
Rise in blood CO 2 content is incorrect. An increase in blood CO 2 content shifts the curve to the right, decreasing oxygen affinity (and aiding oxygen offloading in the tissues).

Rise in plasma temperature
Tidal volume of 250 ml Tidal volume of 250 ml is incorrect. It is far too low. A patient is reviewed in the respiratory clinic with shortness of breath (initially on exertion, but increasing pervasive), a dry hacking cough and fatigue. Direct questioning reveals low level, unintentional weight loss. Which one of the following respiratory physiology tests would be consistent with a diagnosis of moderately established idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

Rise in 2,3-DPG (2,3-diphosphoglycerate)
Total lung capacity of 3.5 litres Total lung capacity of 3.5 litres is incorrect. It is too low.

stem: A patient is reviewed in the respiratory clinic with shortness of breath (initially on exertion, but increasing pervasive), a dry hacking cough and fatigue. Direct questioning reveals low level, unintentional weight loss. Which one of the following respiratory physiology tests would be consistent with a diagnosis of moderately established idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC increased, total lung capacity increased
Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity normal
Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity reduced
Diffusion capacity increased, FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity increased
Diffusion capacity normal, FEV1/FVC reduced, total lung capacity reduced
explanation:
Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity reduced
In restrictive lung disease (such as pulmonary fibrosis as above): diffusion capacity is characteristically decreased FEV 1/FVC ratio is normal or increased total lung capacity is reduced. In obstructive airways disease: FEV 1/FVC is reduced: reversibly in asthma irreversibly in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) total lung capacity is normal or increased.

Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC increased, total lung capacity increased
Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV 1/FVC increased, total lung capacity increased is incorrect. This does not fit into any classical lung pathology.

Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity normal
Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV 1/FVC normal, total lung capacity normal is incorrect. Decreased diffusion capacity with normal other values may represent a pulmonary vascular problem, e.g. pulmonary vasculitis or hypertension.

Diffusion capacity increased, FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity increased
Diffusion capacity increased, FEV 1/FVC normal, total lung capacity increased is incorrect. Increased diffusion capacity is classically seen in alveolar haemorrhage syndromes.

Diffusion capacity normal, FEV1/FVC reduced, total lung capacity reduced
Diffusion capacity normal, FEV 1/FVC reduced, total lung capacity reduced is incorrect. It is not in keeping with any classical lung pathology.

stem: You are evaluating a patient with symptoms consistent with profound arteriopathy. Blood is circulated through the arteries by which one of the following physiological mechanisms?
options: Residual pressure from blood flow through the capillaries
explanation:
Arterial elasticity
The following are all mechanisms for maintaining pressure within the arterial circulation: peripheral arterial elasticity (promotes maintenance of diastolic pressure in arteries and arterioles). ventricular systole recoil of the elastic aorta.

Contraction of external muscles
Contraction of external muscles is incorrect. The question asks about arterial blood flow. The contraction of external muscles promotes venous blood flow.

Negative pressure during inspiration
Negative pressure during inspiration is incorrect. The question asks about arterial blood flow. Negative pressure during inspiration promotes venous blood flow.

Residual pressure from blood flow through the capillaries
Residual pressure from blood flow through the capillaries is incorrect. The question asks about arterial blood flow. The residual pressure from blood flow through the capillaries promotes venous blood flow.

Suction during cardiac diastole
Suction during cardiac diastole is incorrect. The question asks about arterial blood flow. Suction during cardiac diastole promotes venous blood flow.

stem: A 19-year-old girl is seen in the clinic with profound menorrhoea. Initial hormonal blood tests are sent. Which one of the following statements applies to the physiology of the normal menstrual cycle?
options: Rising levels of progesterone occur during the follicular stage
The follicular stage lasts from day 18 to day 28 of the menstrual cycle
The luteal stage lasts from day 1 to day 14 of the menstrual cycle
There is a large fall in GnRH just before ovulation
There is a large rise in GnRH just before ovulation
explanation:
There is a large rise in GnRH just before ovulation
A large pulsatile increase in GnRH does occur just before ovulation.

Rising levels of progesterone occur during the follicular stage
Rising levels of progesterone occur during the follicular stage is incorrect. Rising levels of oestrogens occur during the follicular stage, not progesterone.

The follicular stage lasts from day 18 to day 28 of the menstrual cycle
The follicular stage lasts from day 18 to day 28 of the menstrual cycle is incorrect. The follicular stage lasts from day 1 to day 14 (not 18–28) of the menstrual cycle.

The luteal stage lasts from day 1 to day 14 of the menstrual cycle
The luteal stage lasts from day 1 to day 14 of the menstrual cycle is incorrect. The luteal stage lasts from day 15 to day 28 (not 1–14) of the menstrual cycle.

There is a large fall in GnRH just before ovulation
There is a large fall in GnRH just before ovulation is incorrect. GnRH rises before ovulation, it does not fall.

stem: What is the frequency of alpha waves on an electroencephalography (EEG)?
explanation:
8–13 Hz
Alpha waves have a frequency of 8–13 Hz; their activity normally disappears with attention.

< 4 Hz
< 4 Hz is incorrect. Delta waves have a frequency of < 4 Hz. They are normally seen in sleep in adults and are abnormal in the awake adult.

4–7 Hz
4–7 Hz is incorrect. Theta waves have a frequency of 4–7 Hz. Theta waves are normally seen in sleep at any age.

> 14 Hz
> 14 Hz is incorrect. Beta waves have a frequency of > 14 Hz. Drugs such as barbiturates and benzodiazepines augment Beta waves.

> 20 Hz
> 20 Hz is incorrect. This frequency could indicate a Beta wave.

stem: A 22-year-male student was diagnosed with minimal change nephropathy 4 years previously. He had received short courses of high-dose steroids each time he had a relapse, and had responded promptly. Currently, his sixth relapse (three in the last 6 months) has manifested as ankle oedema. His urinary protein is 5.1g/24 h with an albumin of 21 g/l. Which one of the following treatments is most appropriate in the long term?
explanation:
Cyclophosphamide
Frequent relapses requiring high-dose steroids should prompt treatment with alkylating agents, which usually achieve sustained remission. In this case there are frequent relapses; therefore, cyclophosphamide is the appropriate treatment.

Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor is incorrect. Renal disease with proteinuria > 3 g/24 h requires blood pressure lowering to < 125/75 mmHg, using an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor in preference to other drugs, to prevent progression of disease. However, this person is having multiple relapses in short spaces of time so requires an agent to induce remission rather than one that manages their condition. Patients with nephrotic syndrome are susceptible to thromboembolic disease (some practitioners routinely anticoagulate them), especially where the proteinuria is very heavy. Deep vein thrombosis extending to the inferior vena cava and both renal veins, with pulmonary emboli, may be seen. Children with the nephrotic syndrome, especially due to minimal change disease, are susceptible to infection by capsulated organisms and should be vaccinated against pneumococcus; the susceptibility is multifactorial and probably related to underlying immune deficiencies.

Cyclosporine A
Cyclosporine A is incorrect. Frequently relapsing but steroid-responsive minimal change disease may be controlled by cyclosporine A, but relapse on stopping treatment is frequent.

Nephrectomy
Nephrectomy is incorrect. Nephrectomy is reserved as a last resort for intractable complications of nephrotic syndrome, such as where the protein excretion is leading to severe hypoalbuminemia and massive oedema.

Prednisolone 60 mg/day
Prednisolone 60 mg/day is incorrect. This patient has multiple relapses over the last 6 months; therefore, cyclophosphamide should be commenced.

stem: A 68-year-old man has backache, weight loss and hypercalcaemia. His blood tests reveal elevated plasma globulins at 52 g/l and he has a normocytic anaemia; his 24 h urinary protein excretion is 0.5 g. He develops diarrhoea and vomiting, and presents with acute renal impairment. A renal biopsy is performed. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Light chain nephropathy related to myeloma
explanation:
Light chain nephropathy related to myeloma
This history is typical of myeloma with weight loss, backache and hypercalca emia. Myeloma is an aberrant clone of plasma cells producing immunoglobulin or immunoglobulin light chains. Renal impairment is a major complication of multiple myeloma, found at the time of diagnosis in 20–30% of patients; it occurs in half of patients with myeloma during the course of the disease. However, intratubular casts, composed of light chains, can crystallise within the tubule, leading to oliguric acute kidney disease. Otherwise known as cast nephropathy, myeloma kidney occurs in 30–65% of cases of renal impairment associated with myeloma; this tendency would be exacerbated by hypovolaemia due to a gastroenteric illness.

Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. Acute tubular necrosis may be the result of diarrhoea and vomiting if there has been hypotension; however, in this case, it would not fit with the previous history suggestive of myeloma.

Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is incorrect. AL amyloidosis could occur in myeloma and cause renal impairment, but would usually be heralded by more significant proteinuria (often nephrotic range). Amyloidosis is usually lambda subtype light chain, occurring in 20% of patients with renal impairment in myeloma.

Interstitial nephritis
Interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Interstitial nephritis is often associated with initiation of medications, such as antibiotics or proton pump inhibitors; it is not associated with myeloma and does not fit this clinical picture.

Intraglomerular thrombi
Intraglomerular thrombi is incorrect. Intraglomerular thrombi of immunoglobulins may occur, but this is very rare; it has been described in malignant lymphoma. The clinical picture would include nephrotic syndrome and systemic lymphadenopathy. Renal biopsy will reveal massive deposition of amorphous material in the glomerular capillary lumens. The patient is not nephrotic in this case.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with a three-month history of diarrhoea with stools that float and are difficult to flush away, usually following food. He has also been tiring easily and complains of abdominal bloating. On direct questioning he admits to 6kg of weight loss. These features are suggestive of malabsorption. Which one of the following investigations would have the potential to indicate a single cause for this?
options: Pancreolauryl test (comparison of the absorption of fluorescein and fluorescein dilaurate)
explanation:
Lactose tolerance test
Involving a comparison in blood glucose rise following a dose of lactose compared with a dose of glucose, the test is specific for lactase deficiency, the only likely single cause here. Definitive diagnosis of lactose intolerance is by measurement of lactase of a biopsy sample. Lactose intolerance symptoms include weight loss and malabsorption.

Breath hydrogen measurement
Breath hydrogen measurement is incorrect. Breath hydrogen excretion, is increased with increased bacterial activity in the gut, but this can be a cause of malabsorption (colonisation of the small gut causes deconjugation of bile salts) and also a consequence (fermentation of unabsorbed nutrients in the large intestine).

Faecal fat excretion
Faecal fat excretion is incorrect. The measurement of faecal fat excretion (now regarded as obsolete by many physicians) may indicate malabsorption, but it does not distinguish between its possible causes, making this incorrect. The remaining tests may indicate the broad type of pathology, but not a specific cause.

Pancreolauryl test (comparison of the absorption of fluorescein and fluorescein dilaurate)
Pancreolauryl test (comparison of the absorption of fluorescein and fluorescein dilaurate) is incorrect. The pancreolauryl test can be abnormal in a range of pancreatic and biliary diseases.

Xylose tolerance test
Xylose tolerance test is incorrect. The xylose absorption test, is also incorrect as the absorption of xylose may be decreased in various small intestinal diseases.

stem: A 20-year-old man is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic because of delayed puberty. On examination, he has a preadolescent body habitus and no evidence of the development of secondary sexual characteristics. Serum testosterone, luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentrations are all in the prepubertal range. The LH and FSH concentrations increase only slightly following a single injection of gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) but a normal response is elicited after GnRH is given daily for seven consecutive days. Which one of the following is most likely to be the cause of his delayed puberty?
explanation:
A hypothalamic disorder
A poor response to a single injection of GnRH implies pituitary failure or chronic under stimulation of the pituitary due to a lack of hypothalamic GnRH (resulting in decreased pituitary sensitivity to the hypothalamic hormone.

A pituitary disorder
A pituitary disorder is incorrect. Normal pituitary response after 7 days of GnRH suggests that the mechanism for the secretion of FSH and LH by the pituitary is intact, implicating the hypothalamus.

Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome is incorrect. In Klinefelter syndrome (46XXY) the lack of negative feedback leads to increased gonadotrophin concentrations not reduced.

Mumps orchitis in childhood
Mumps orchitis in childhood is also incorrect. In testicular failure due to mumps orchitis, the same lack of negative feedback would raise not reduce gonadotrophins.

Seminiferous tubular dysfunction
Seminiferous tubular dysfunction is incorrect. In seminiferous tubule dysfunction, the plasma follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentration tends to be elevated; spermatogenesis is reduced or absent but masculinisation is normal.

stem: A 32-year-old man receives a tetanus booster after cutting his hand whilst gardening. Within 10 minutes he has a severe local erythematous reaction, followed soon after by generalised erythema, stridor, nausea and hypotension. He responded to fluid resuscitation, hydrocortisone, antihistamines and subcutaneous adrenaline. Patch testing later demonstrated an immediate reaction to both diphtheria and tetanus toxoid. Which one of the following types of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
explanation:
Type I
The clinical picture and positive patch testing together support a diagnosis of type I (immediate) hypersensitivity. Patch or radioallergosorbent testing (RAST) after reaction to vaccination is important: many vaccines share common components e.g. antibiotics or preservatives, and route of production (e.g. influenza vaccines produced in hen’s eggs). Type I hypersensitivity is driven by antigen-specific IgE antibodies which bind to receptors on the surface of mast cells and basophils. Development of hypersensitivity requires presensitisation to the antigen, in this case from previous tetanus vaccination.

Type II
Type II is incorrect. Type II or cytotoxic, antibody dependent (IgM, IgG) hypersensitivity is classical of the transfusion reactions.

Type III
Type III is incorrect. Type III or immune complex hypersensitivity involves arthus reactions or serum sickness.

Type IV
Type IV is incorrect. Type IV or delayed hypersensitivity – slow to develop as the name suggests - includes processes such as transplant rejection, contact dermatitis and TB.

Type V
Type V is incorrect. The classic Coombs and Gell classification contains just the above four types.

stem: You are taking part in studies of a potential new artificial lung surfactant and are interested in how its chemical construct compares with endogenous lung surfactant. What does endogenous lung surfactant mainly consist of?
explanation:
Phospholipoproteins
Surfactant consists predominantly of phospholipids (80%) such as dipalmitoylphosphadidylcholine (40%), cholesterol (8%) and apolipoproteins (5%), known as SP-A to D. The apolipoproteins form a complex with dipalmitolyphosphatidylcholine and other phospholipoproteins. The main function of surfactant is to increase pulmonary compliance and lead to a reduction in atelectasis. Both animal-derived and synthetic surfactants are now available for the treatment of a range of diseases.

Cholesterol
Cholesterol is incorrect. Cholesterol makes up only 8% of endogenous lung surfactant.

Free water
Free water is incorrect. Surfactant free water is relatively low.

Peptides
Peptides is incorrect. Proteins other than apolipoproteins constitute approximately 5%.

Triglyceride
Triglyceride is incorrect. Triglycerides constitute a minimal proportion of surfactant.

stem: She is treated with 3% saline, but when the nurses go in to her the following morning they notice she is unable to move. You suspect central pontine myelinolysis. When considering the intracellular compartment what has occurred?
explanation:
Loss of water
When sodium is corrected – especially if rapidly – the extracellular fluid becomes relatively hypertonic. This leads to loss of water from the intracellular compartment. The exact mechanism that leads to preferential loss of myelin is not known. Slow correction of sodium is preferred, and normal or twice-normal saline should be reserved for emergency situations such as multiple seizures.

Gain in Na
Gain in Na is incorrect. The extracellular not intracellular compartment will initially gain Na. Whilst the intracellular compartment will slowly equilibrate with extracellular Na over time, this is not responsible for the above pathology.

Gain in Na and water
Gain in Na and water is incorrect. The gain in Na and water refers to the extracellular compartment.

Gain in water
Gain in Na and water is incorrect. The gain in water, is incorrect as it refers to the extra- not intracellular compartment.
