You are examining a new treatment for blood pressure the route of excretion for which is thought to involve the sodium chloride renal symporter. Which of the following drugs used in the treatment of hypertension or cardiac failure acts directly on the sodium chloride renal symporter?

Loss in Na
Loss in Na is incorrect. Over time the intracellular compartment will also gain sodium not lose it.

stem: In your role as the Renal Registrar, you are reviewing pathologies involved in chronic renal dysfunction. Which of the following correctly describes one of the principal actions of endothelin on the kidney?
explanation:
Afferent arteriole vasoconstriction
Endothelin preferentially constricts afferent arterioles. In addition it: Stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system Leads to release of atrial natriuretic peptide Inhibits the action of vasopressin Two types of endothelin receptor have been characterised, A and B. Binding of endothelin to the A receptor induces vasoconstriction, binding to the B receptor leads to nitric oxide release and hence vasodilatation.

Afferent arteriole vasodilatation
Afferent arteriole vasodilitation is incorrect. Efferent arteriole vasoconstriction is particularly mediated by angiotensin-II, to defend GFR in states of generalised vasoconstriction and reduced blood flow.

Efferent arteriole vasodilatation
Efferent arteriole vasodilatation is incorrect. In contrast, efferent arteriole vasodilation will occur when angiotensin-II levels fall.

Potentiation of vasopressin action
Potentiation of vasopressin action is incorrect. Vasopressin is not potentiated by endogenous peptides. 16 65 You are examining the function of prostaglandins. Which of the following fits with what is known about prostaglandins?

Sodium retention
Sodium retention is incorrect. Whilst afferent vasoconstriction will reduce GFR and thus sodium excretion, this is an indirect effect not a principal action making.

stem: An 18-year-old man attends the transplant clinic with his brother, who has chronic kidney disease due to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). He would like to donate a kidney to his brother if possible. Which one of the following is the most appropriate modality for screening?
explanation:
Genetic screening
There are two types of ADPKD: type 1 disease makes up around 85–90% of the cases; type 2 disease makes up the remainder. The major indication for genetic screening in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is for subjects who are considering donating a kidney to a relative affected by the disease. Genetic probes exist for both mutations, the causative mutation for type 1 being found on chromosome 16 and type 2 on chromosome 4.

Abdominal ultrasound scan
Abdominal ultrasound scan is incorrect. Although abdominal ultrasound has a high degree of sensitivity for ADPKD type 1, the sensitivity for ADPKD type 2 is much lower, and it is possible that a subject may be cleared to donate a kidney yet still have the disease.

Computed tomography (CT) scan
Computed tomography (CT) scan is incorrect. Similar to ultrasound scan, computer tomography may not be sensitive enough to detect patients with type 2 ADPKD who may still have the disease.

Intravenous urography
Intravenous urography is incorrect. Intravenous urography would not be useful in this case as it is likely to be normal in patients with ADPKD. This investigation is appropriate in identifying renal calculi and urinary obstruction.

Micturating cystogram
Micturating cystogram is incorrect. Micturating cystogram is used in cases to investigate for vesicoureteric reflux. It would be normal in ADPKD.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is managed with long-term haemodialysis. The cause of her chronic kidney disease is long-standing type 1 diabetes. She is treated with a steady dose of erythropoietin (EPO), yet on recent dialysis sessions you have noticed a decrease in her Hb from 11.1 g/dl post EPO 4 weeks or more ago, to 8.4 g/dl at her last dialysis session. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Serum ferritin
Patients with chronic kidney disease often have coexistent low iron stores. Adequate total body iron is required for erythropoietin to work as an effective treatment for renal anaemia. Options for screening include serum ferritin, percentage hypochromia and transferring saturation. Intravenous iron replacement is now established as a treatment of choice for iron replacement. Untreated, chronic anaemia is thought to predispose to worsening of left ventricular hypertrophy in this group of patients.

Bone marrow aspiration
Bone marrow aspiration is incorrect. Bone marrow aspiration is invasive and not indicated in this case. It would be an investigation of choice in cases of blood dyscrasias and malignancies, but there is no indication of this in this scenario.

Lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy
Lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is incorrect. Lower GI endoscopy may be required if there are any red flag symptoms of malignancy such as weight loss, change in bowel habit and loss of appetite. It may be required in this case if there is no iron deficiency and a resistance of haemoglobin to EPO; however, it would not be the next most appropriate investigation in this case.

Measurement of EPO antibodies
Measurement of EPO antibodies is incorrect. EPO antibodies is present in pure red cell aplasia, which is an isolated disorder to erythropoiesis that leads to sudden, progressive, severe anaemia of sudden onset. It is rare and would not be the first investigation in this case.

Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy
Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is incorrect. Upper GI endoscopy may be required if there is a further drop in haemoglobin and resistance to EPO therapy. It would not be the first investigation of choice in this case. 19 You review a 68-year-old gentleman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in the respiratory clinic. Despite optimisation of his inhaled therapy, he has required daily high-dose steroid all winter to keep his symptoms under control. On examination you note a moon face, copious striae and early limb muscle wasting. His BP is 155/90 mmHg.

stem: You review a 68-year-old gentleman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in the respiratory clinic. Despite optimisation of his inhaled therapy, he has required daily high-dose steroid all winter to keep his symptoms under control. On examination you note a moon face, copious striae and early limb muscle wasting. His BP is 155/90 mmHg. Which of the following is the likely status of his endogenous corticosteroid axis?
explanation:
Low ACTH
This patient has features of corticosteroid excess against a background of oral steroid use. As such a reduction in both ACTH and endogenous cortisol production is likely. This increases the risk of adrenal crisis with any intercurrent serious illness.

Elevated aldosterone
Elevated aldosterone is incorrect. If anything aldosterone levels are likely to be at the lower end of the normal range because of corticosteroid driven salt and water retention.

Elevated cortisol
Elevated cortisol is incorrect. Cortisol levels are likely to be suppressed because of exogenous steroid administration.

High ACTH
High ACTH is incorrect. Against a picture of corticosteroid excess low rather than high ACTH levels would be seen.

Normal ACTH
Normal ACTH is incorrect. ACTH levels are suppressed in the presence of both endogenous and exogenous corticosteroid excess.

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the Well Man Clinic for review of his blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes management. He is advised about a low-sugar, low-salt, low-fat diet. Which of the following is the UK recommended daily maximum for salt in the diet?
explanation:
6g
In the UK, 6 g is the recommended daily maximum for salt intake. Advice is given that foods containing >1.5 g/100 g of salt are considered high-salt foods, while those containing <0.3 g/100 g are low-salt foods. Maximum saturated fat intake is recommended to be 30 g/day for men and 20 g/day for women. With respect to sugars, high-sugar foods are those containing >22.5 g/100 g of sugar, while low-sugar foods are those containing 5 g/100 g of sugar or less.

3g
3g 3 g is incorrect. 3 g of salt intake is within the normal recommended intake.

1g
1g 1 g is incorrect. 1 g of salt intake is within the normal recommended intake.

12 g
12 g is incorrect. 12 g of salt intake twice exceeds the daily recommended intake.

18 g
18 g is incorrect. 18 g of daily salt intake far exceeds the daily recommendation. Excessive intake of salt is thought to lead to fluid accumulation and increased blood pressure, with negative long-term effects on the cardiovascular system. An 18 year old attempts to climb Mount Everest as a fundraising project during his gap year. Despite extensive training at sea level, his attempt has to be paused due to a combination of headache, dizziness and shortness of breath. After two days at the same level, his symptoms resolve and he is able to push on to the summit.

stem: An 18 year old attempts to climb Mount Everest as a fundraising project during his gap year. Despite extensive training at sea level, his attempt has to be paused due to a combination of headache, dizziness and shortness of breath. After two days at the same level, his symptoms resolve and he is able to push on to the summit. Which of the following is involved in high altitude acclimatisation?
explanation:
Increased pulmonary perfusion
Above 14 000 ft (4267 m) the heart rate, cardiac output and pulmonary artery pressure increase (increasing pulmonary perfusion).

Alveolar hypoventilation
Alveolar hypoventilation is incorrect. Physiological acclimatisation starts at about 7000 ft (2100m). The partial pressure of atmospheric O 2 reduces with altitude. Acclimatisation involves the following changes, serving to maintain arterial O 2 tension. Pulmonary ventilation and perfusion increase (not decrease).

Decreased renal excretion of bicarbonate
Decreased renal excretion of bicarbonate is incorrect. Renal excretion of bicarbonate actually increases as a short-term adaptation to high altitude living.

Decreased haematocrit
Decreased haematocrit is incorrect. Erythrocyte production increases; haemoglobin and haematocrit increase.

Increased plasma volume
Increased plasma volume is incorrect. Plasma volume reduces as an adaptation to altitude. It increases again when patients return to sea level. Measured stroke volume also decreases in patients at high altitude.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with suspected emphysema comes to the Respiratory Clinic to discuss the results of her respiratory function tests. Residual volume is significantly prolonged. Which of the following correctly describes the residual volume?
options: The maximum amount of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximum inhalation
The volume of air displaced between normal inhalation and exhalation when extra effort is not
The volume of air that remains in the lungs after maximum forceful expiration
The volume of air that can be forced out in 1 s after taking a deep breath (FEV 1)
The additional volume of air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal tidal volume
explanation:
The volume of air that remains in the lungs after maximum forceful expiration
The residual volume is the volume of air that remains in the lungs after maximum forceful expiration. Residual volume is typically increased in patients with emphysema, where because of airway dilatation a large volume of air remains in the lungs.

The maximum amount of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximum inhalation
This is the vital capacity, the maximum amount of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximum inhalation. It is equal to the sum of inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume. Vital capacity is decreased in restrictive lung disease; in obstructive lung disease, it is normal or slightly reduced.

The volume of air displaced between normal inhalation and exhalation when extra effort is not
The volume of air displaced between normal inhalation and exhalation when extra effort is not applied This is the tidal volume, volume of air displaced between normal inhalation and exhalation when extra effort is not applied. Low tidal volume is an option in mechanical ventilation where it may prevent progressive lung damage as a result of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

The volume of air that can be forced out in 1 s after taking a deep breath (FEV 1)
The FEV 1 is the volume of air that can be forced out in 1 s after taking a deep breath. It is useful in the assessment of obstructive lung diseases such as asthma, including response to therapy.

The additional volume of air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal tidal volume
The inspiratory reserve volume is the additional volume of air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal tidal volume. Inspiratory reserve volume decreases with increased work of breathing, for example during extreme exercise.

stem: You are called to the Intensive Therapy Unit to see a 65-year-old patient who requires controlled mechanical ventilation after major non-cardiac surgery but is becoming hypoxaemic when the F iO 2 is reduced from 0.4 to 0.3. He has a complex peri-operative course and a peri-op MI is diagnosed. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Cardiac index and oxygen delivery correlate well with outcome from high-risk surgery
Measurement of mixed venous oxygen saturation (SVO2) requires a pulmonary venous (PV) catheter
Pre- or perioperative β-blockade should be commenced to survival after major non-cardiac
Simple indices of circulatory status – such as urine output, blood pressure and central venous
Survivors after major surgery decrease their cardiac index and oxygen delivery in the perioperative
explanation:
Cardiac index and oxygen delivery correlate well with outcome from high-risk surgery
Cardiac index is of course a measure of left ventricular reserve to cope with haemodynamic shifts associated with major surgery and oxygen delivery an indicator of risk of tissue hypoxia. Both these measures together are an accurate measure of risk of poor outcome from high risk surgery.

Measurement of mixed venous oxygen saturation (SVO2) requires a pulmonary venous (PV) catheter
Measurement of mixed venous oxygen saturation (SVO2) requires a pulmonary venous (PV) catheter to sample pulmonary capillary blood Measurement of mixed venous oxygen saturation (S VO 2) requires a pulmonary venous (PV) catheter to sample pulmonary capillary blood is incorrect. Measurement of mixed venous oxygen saturation (S VO 2) requires a pulmonary artery (PA) catheter to sample pulmonary capillary blood (not venous).

Pre- or perioperative β-blockade should be commenced to survival after major non-cardiac
Pre- or perioperative β-blockade should be commenced to survival after major non-cardiac surgery in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease Pre- or perioperative β-blockade should be commenced to survival after major non-cardiac surgery in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease is incorrect. It has been historically controversial but has now been shown to be incorrect. There has been much interest in the anaesthesia literature in using highly selective preor perioperative β-blockade to survival after major non-cardiac surgery in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease, e.g. previous heart failure, moderate hypertension and myocardial infarction (MI). Early trials, including multi-centre data, using a regime started 48–72 h preoperatively and continued for 14–28 days post-surgery, showed promise in reducing complications such as peri-operative MI. However, subsequent meta-analyses have questioned the validity of these effects, and furthermore found significantly increased risk of stroke, death, hypotension and bradycardia. Current pragmatic best practice therefore supports continuing pre-existing therapy, but not commencing β-blockade in the perioperative period.

Simple indices of circulatory status – such as urine output, blood pressure and central venous
Simple indices of circulatory status – such as urine output, blood pressure and central venous pressure– correlate better with operative risk in high-risk non-cardiac surgery than a history of previous cardiovascular disease Simple indices of circulatory status – such as urine output, blood pressure and central venous pressure– correlate better with operative risk in high-risk non-cardiac surgery than a history of previous cardiovascular disease is incorrect. Simple indices of circulatory status – such as urine output, blood pressure and central venous pressure – correlate poorly with outcome from high-risk surgery compared with previous cardiac history.

Survivors after major surgery decrease their cardiac index and oxygen delivery in the perioperative.

stem: You are reviewing the mode of action of a new antihypertensive drug, which is said to have a partial thiazidelike action. Upon which part of the kidney are thiazide diuretics thought to act?
explanation:
Distal convoluted tubule
Thiazide diuretics are excreted into the lumen of the distal tubule, where they block reabsorption of chloride into distal tubular cells, so also preventing reabsorption of sodium

Ascending loop of Henle
Ascending loop of Henle is incorrect. Furosemide exerts its primary mode of action by inhibiting the sodiumpotassium-chloride transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

Collecting duct
Collecting duct is incorrect. Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.

Descending loop of Henle
Descending loop of Henle is incorrect. Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.

Proximal convoluted tubule.

stem: Which one of the following would you propose initially to manage his sodium levels?
explanation:
Fluid restriction
In cases of hyponatraemia, fluid restriction may be considered as an initial step if the patient is asymptomatic or has mild symptoms of hyponatraemia. If the patient fails to respond or sequalae develop such as seizures, then either demeclocycline or hypertonic saline may be possible next step options, taking care to only raise sodium by around 8–10 mmol/ over a 24-h period. A gentle approach is favoured initially as it is difficult to ascertain if the patient's hyponatraemia is acute or chronic in this case.

1.8% saline fluid replacement
1.8% saline fluid replacement is incorrect. In cases of hyponatraemia, fluid restriction as an initial step should be considered if the patient is asymptomatic or has only mild symptoms. If the patient fails to respond or sequalae develop such as seizures, then either demeclocycline or hypertonic saline may be possible options.

3% saline fluid replacement
3% saline fluid replacement is incorrect. In patients with profound hyponatraemia with moderately severe symptoms, a single intravenous infusion of 150 ml 3% hypertonic saline or equivalent over 20 minutes is indicated. Care must be taken care to only raise sodium by around 8–10 mmol/l over a 24-h period so this should ideally occur in a higher care facility with frequent laboratory monitoring. Too rapid a correction of serum sodium may precipitate central pontine myelinolysis.

Demeclocycline
Demeclocycline is incorrect. If the patient fails to respond to fluid restriction or sequalae develop such as seizures, then either demeclocycline or hypertonic saline may be possible options, taking care to only raise sodium by around 8–10 mmol/ over a 24-h period. The question asks what to try first and both 3% saline and demeclocycline are rescue options when fluid retention fails as a treatment.

Furosemide IV.

stem: A 53-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of feeling non-specifically unwell and has recently noticed a rash on his legs and feet. He is breathless and has had a single episode of haemoptysis; he has a 30pack/year smoking history. His Hb is 94 g/l, urinalysis shows dipstick haematuria and proteinuria and midstream urine reveals 100 red blood cells/hpf with no white blood cells. The most likely explanation for the pulmonary symptoms is?
explanation:
Pulmonary haemorrhage
The midstream urine sample excludes infection, confirming the abnormal urinalysis to be due to glomerulonephritis; microscopy of fresh urine may demonstrate red cell casts. This is a classical history for small vessel vasculitis, leading to pulmonary renal syndrome, which may be due to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis or anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture’s disease if, as in this case, pulmonary haemorrhage is seen). Patients with pulmonary involvement in systemic vasculitis typically develop alveolar capillaritis, resulting in alveolar haemorrhage. Pulmonary haemorrhage in vasculitis is more common in smokers.

Bronchogenic carcinoma
Bronchogenic carcinoma is incorrect. Older patients with membranous nephropathy may have an underlying malignancy, which should be sought carefully; however, this does not usually cause haematuria. In this patient, a bronchogenic carcinoma is clearly high on the differential diagnosis list.

Pneumococcal pneumonia
Pneumococcal pneumonia is incorrect. Pneumococcal pneumonia may present with haemoptysis, but would not present with haematoproteinuria.

Pulmonary embolus
Pulmonary embolus is incorrect. Pulmonary embolus may also present with haemoptysis, but it is not an associated feature of vasculitis.

Pulmonary oedema
Pulmonary oedema is incorrect. Although kidney disease may result in pulmonary oedema, the haemoptysis is often mixed with frothy sputum, and would not account for the anaemia and rash as present in this case.

stem: You review a 74-year-old man who has been feeling tired and lethargic over the past few months. His Hb is 94 g/l and he has a raised mean cell volume. You check his autoantibodies and he has positive intrinsic factor antibodies. Which one of the following represents the location of intrinsic factor production?
explanation:
Fundus of the stomach
Intrinsic factor is produced by parietal cells which are found in the fundus of the stomach. Parietal cells are also responsible for the production of hydrochloric acid

Cardia of the stomach
Cardia of the stomach is incorrect. The stomach cardia is mostly responsible for secreting mucous.

First part of the duodenum
First part of the duodenum is incorrect. Whilst antibodies in the duodenum prevent small bowel absorption of B12, this is not where intrinsic factor is produced.

Ileum
Ileum is incorrect. Whilst intrinsic factor is produced in the stomach, it is essential for the absorption of B12 in the small bowel, hence antibodies found here lead to a lack of intrinsic factor and macrocytic anaemia.

Second part of the duodenum.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of central, crushing chest pain radiating to her jaw. As a myocardial infarction is suspected, an ECG is immediately taken. ST elevation and Q waves are present in leads V 4–V 6, I and AVL. Which one of the following aspects of the heart is most likely to have been involved in the infarct?
explanation:
Anterolateral
This combination (ST elevation and Q waves present in leads V 4–V 6, I and AVL) suggests a anterolateral infarct.

Anterior
Anterior is incorrect. Anterior infarcts tend to involve the chest leads only (typically V 2–V 5)

Anteroseptal
Anteroseptal is incorrect. Anteroseptal infarcts involve V 1–V 3

Inferior
Inferior is incorrect. Inferior infarcts involve II, III and AVF.

stem: You are reviewing the results of arterial blood gases in the chemical pathology laboratory. Which one of the following results is most likely to be a laboratory error?
explanation:
pH 7.40; HCO3- 15 mmol/l; PaCO2 5.5 mmol/l
Bicarbonate is only 15 mmol/l, and there is a PaCO2 of 5.5, therefore the pH cannot possibly be 7.40. The pH must be in the acidotic range. Indeed, calculating pH using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives a value of 7.18.

pH 7.17; HCO3- 17 mmol/l; PaCO2 6.5 mmol/l
pH 7.17; HCO3- 17 mmol/l; PaCO2 6.5 mmol/l is incorrect. It is consistent with a mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis.

pH 7.28; HCO3- 17 mmol/l; PaCO2 5 mmol/l
pH 7.28; HCO3- 17 mmol/l; PaCO2 5 mmol/l is incorrect. It is consistent with a metabolic acidosis.

pH 7.49; HCO3- 23 mmol/l; PaCO2 4.2 mmol/l
pH 7.49; HCO3- 23 mmol/l; PaCO2 4.2 mmol/l is incorrect. It has a normal bicarbonate, but the PaCO2 is low, consistent with a respiratory alkalotic picture.

pH 7.53; HCO3- 33 mmol/l; PaCO2 5.5 mmol/l
pH 7.53;.

stem: Some 4 h after sustaining major trauma in a road traffic collision, a 22-year-old man, not known to have diabetes, is found to have a high blood glucose concentration. Increased secretion of which one of the following substances is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Adrenaline (epinephrine)
During the metabolic response to trauma, there is increased secretion of: 1. catecholamines 2. cortisol 3. glucagon 4. growth hormone. Catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon act directly to increase blood glucose concentration. 1. Adrenaline and glucagon act most rapidly, by stimulating glycogenolysis; this makes adrenaline the correct answer at the 4-h mark. 2. Cortisol tends to act more slowly, through the stimulation of gluconeogenesis. C-reactive protein is a marker of inflammation, but does not affect glucose homeostasis. Growth hormone appears to potentiate the action of cortisol and opposes the action ofChat insulin; again with this would contribute to a later rise in blood glucose. Insulin is a hypoglycaemic hormone. The degree of the neuroendocrine stress response is related to the severity of the trauma and the time lapse before treatment (fluid replacement, pain relief etc) is instituted. Hyperglycaemia can persist for many hours and even days in some cases.

Cortisol
Cortisol is incorrect. Cortisol acts directly to increase blood glucose but tends to act more slowly, through stimulation of gluconeogenesis.

C-reactive protein
C-reactive protein is incorrect. C-reactive protein is a marker of inflammation, but does not affect glucose homeostasis.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. Growth hormone appears to potentiate the action of cortisol and opposes the action of insulin, this would contribute to a later rise in blood glucose.

stem: What is the most likely reason for these results?
explanation:
Pregnancy
The arterial blood gas (ABG) shows a respiratory alkalosis. This results from hyperventilation as excess elimination of CO2 causes a rise in the blood pH. Potential causes include: Catastrophic central nervous system (CNS) event e.g. haemorrhage Drugs (salicylates, progesterone) Pregnancy, with increased magnitude as gestation progresses Decreased lung compliance (interstitial lung disease) Anxiety Hepatic failure

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline in excess causes a metabolic acidosis. This would be an acute phenomena.

Cushing syndrome
Cushing syndrome is incorrect. Cushing syndrome would cause weight gain, but any effect on ventilation would likely be towards hypoventilation due to respiratory muscle weakness

Hepatic failure
Hepatic failure is incorrect. Other clinical and biochemical abnormalities would be expected in hepatic failure. Also amenorrhoea would not be common.

stem: You are reviewing possible new anti-arrhythmic agents, and looking at those which may impact on cardiac action potential repolarisation. Closure of which type of ion channel is responsible for the rapid repolarisation phase (phase 3)?
explanation:
Calcium
During phase 3 of the cardiac action potential, closure of L-type calcium channels occurs. This leads to a net outward current, allowing more potassium channels to open. L-type calcium channel blockers include cardioselective calcium antagonists such as diltiazem and verapamil. These are class IV anti-arrhythmics that by definition prolong phase 2 of the action potential (delaying phase 3). During phase 2, also known as the plateau phase, the membrane action potential remains constant due to no net movement of ions in and out of the cell. Two ion channels are of particular interest here: Potassium channels Calcium channels The potassium channels open up, allowing the ions to move out of the cell. However, the cell does not repolarize because the calcium channels open up as well and the net effect is a stable membrane potential. During phase 3, the calcium channels close while the potassium channels remain open. This allows for a net outward current and the cell membrane repolarizes. The state of potassium channels remains the same in phase 2 and 3, whereas, the closure of calcium channels during phase 3 causes results in repolarization.

Chloride
Chloride is incorrect. Cardiac chloride channels are generally not active under normal action potential conditions.

Magnesium
Magnesium is incorrect. Magnesium promotes the movement of calcium, sodium and potassium and stabilises membrane potentials.

Potassium
Potassium is incorrect. Slow delayed-rectifier potassium channels remain open during phase 3.

stem: You are examining a new treatment for blood pressure the route of excretion for which is thought to involve the sodium chloride renal symporter. Which of the following drugs used in the treatment of hypertension or cardiac failure acts directly on the sodium chloride renal symporter?
explanation:
Bendroflumethiazide
Thiazide diuretics block the sodium chloride renal symporter (AKA sodiuchloride cotransporter). A loss of function mutation in the symporter results in Gitelmann’s syndrome which mimics the hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis seen with thiazides.

Enalapril
Enalapril is incorrect. Enalapril acts via the angiotensin system.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. Furosemide inhibits the luminal sodium-potassium-chloride symporter in the thick ascending limb of the Loop of Henle.

Losartan
Losartan is incorrect. Losartan acts via the angiotensin system.

stem: A researcher is examining a potential new anti-arrhythmic that impacts phase 0 of the cardiac action potential. Shifts in which of the following ions are responsible for phase 0 of the cardiac action potential in cardiac myocytes?
explanation:
Sodium
A rapid influx of sodium ions is responsible for phase 0 of the cardiac action potential. Class I antiarrythmics are sodium channel blockers which depress phase 0 and have variable affects on repolarization. This class includes: Ia: Procainamide Ib: Lidocaine Ic: Flecanide

Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is incorrect. Bicarbonate movement is not implicated in cardiac action potentials.

Calcium
Calcium is incorrect. Influx of calcium is responsible for phase 2. Class IV anti-arrhythmics block L-type calcium channels, prolong phase 2 and include diltiazem and verapamil.

Chloride
Chloride is incorrect. Cardiac chloride channels are generally not active under normal action potential conditions.

stem: You are examining the function of prostaglandins. Which of the following fits with what is known about prostaglandins?
options: Cyclo-oxygenases are responsible for prostaglandin breakdown
They are synthesised from amino acids
They bind to G protein coupled receptors
explanation:
They bind to G protein coupled receptors
Prostaglandins bind to G protein coupled receptors and have a wide range of actions, including on: Vascular smooth muscle cells Platelet function Sensitisation to pain Calcium metabolism Glomerular filtration rate

Aspirin stimulates production of prostaglandin
Aspirin stimulates production of prostaglandin is incorrect. Aspirin (and glucocorticoids) inhibit prostaglandin synthesis.

Cyclo-oxygenases are responsible for prostaglandin breakdown
Cyclo-oxygenases are responsible for prostaglandin breakdown is incorrect. Cyclooxygenase is responsible for prostaglandin synthesis, not breakdown.

They are synthesised from amino acids
They are synthesised from amino acids is incorrect. Prostaglandins are biosynthesised from straight-chain C20 fatty acids, arachidonic acid being the precursor, not amino acids.

They bind to steroid receptors.

stem: Hypoxia leads to differentiated effects on the vascular beds of the body. Some vascular beds will demonstrate vasoconstriction, others vasodilation. Which of the following vascular beds vasoconstrict in response to hypoxia?
explanation:
Pulmonary
The pulmonary vasculature vasoconstricts in response to hypoxia, allowing blood to be redirected to areas of the lung with higher oxygen levels. This improves the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio. The acute vascular response to hypoxia is thought to be mediated by nitric oxide (NO). Systemic reaction to hypoxia is an increase in sympathetic tone, which leads to vasoconstriction; however in the vital body organs (such as the brain, heart, kidneys and intestines) local mediators cause vasodilation in the vascular bed to maintain sufficient glucose and oxygen supply. Within the pulmonary vasculature, hypoxia induces sustained vasoconstriction which redirects blood flow to areas of the lungs that are relatively oxygen rich. This limits the amount of blood passing through the lungs that is not oxygenated; ie it improves the VQ ratio.

Cerebral
Cerebral is incorrect. The cerebral vascular bed vasodilates in response to hypoxia in order to conserve glucose and oxygen supply to this vital organ. This is mediated by a combination of vasoactive metabolites and direct effect of hypoxia on the endothelium.

Coronary
Coronary is incorrect. The coronary vascular bed vasodilates in response to hypoxia in order to supply sufficient glucose and oxygen to this vital organ.

Intestinal
Intestinal is incorrect. In fact the vascular bed vasodilates in response to hypoxia to maintain sufficient oxygen supply to the intestines, prevent life-threatening ischaemia.

Renal
Renal is incorrect. The renal vasculature vasodilates under hypoxic conditions, maintaining perfusion of this vital organ.

stem: A 62-year-old man sees his GP for the slow, insidious onset of a tremor in his left arm. Direct questioning reveals several months of constipation and low mood. Examination confirms asymmetrical tremor in conjunction with subtle bradykinesia and rigidity. The primary neurochemical disturbance in idiopathic Parkinson’s disease involves which one of the following?
explanation:
Dopamine
The pathogenesis of Parkinson’s disease is multifactorial. It is characterised by a progressive death of heterogeneous populations of neurones, particularly in the substantia nigra, resulting in a regional loss of the neurotransmitter dopamine (60–70% loss of neurones occurs prior to the emergence of symptoms). The role of the substantia nigra in movement is illustrated by the motor symptoms a loss of dopamine at this site produces.

Adrenaline
Adrenaline is incorrect. Adrenaline is a catecholine. Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal medulla in response to metabolic or global homeostatic changes.

γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA)
γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is incorrect. GABA is the chief inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.

Noradrenaline
Noradrenaline is incorrect. Noradrenaline is a catecholine. Noradrenaline is the predominant neurotransmitter in the sympathetic nervous system, and is essential for cardiovascular function.

Substance P
Substance P is incorrect. Substance P acts as a neurotransmitter at sensory nerves, implicated in pain and inflammation.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a long history of alcohol abuse is admitted to hospital with acute abdominal pain and is diagnosed clinically as having acute pancreatitis. This is confirmed by finding a high serum amylase activity and by the results of an ultrasound scan. He has not had a similar illness before. His serum is seen to be lipaemic: serum triglyceride concentration is 26 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the hypertriglyceridaemia?
explanation:
Increased synthesis of VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein)
The association is due to the increased synthesis of triglyceride for incorporation into very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in the liver. This occurs because chronic use of alcohol drives increased fat synthesis, including within the liver itself.

Decreased pancreatic lipase secretion
Decreased pancreatic lipase secretion is incorrect. High not reduced plasma levels of pancreatic lipase are found in pancreatitis. Moreover this does not affect the metabolism of lipoproteins.

Deficiency of apolipoprotein C-II
Deficiency of apolipoprotein C-II is incorrect. Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency is rare, inherited causes of severe hypertriglyceridaemia, which usually present in childhood.

Deficiency of LDL (low-density lipoprotein) receptors
Deficiency of LDL receptors is incorrect. Deficiency of LDL receptors (involved in transport of cholesterol intracellularly from the plasma) is the cause of familial hypercholesterolaemia, not associated with alcohol excess. Lipoprotein lipase is responsible for the clearance of VLDL and chylomicrons from the plasma: it is activated by apolipoprotein C-II.

Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase
Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase is incorrect. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency is rare, inherited causes of severe hypertriglyceridaemia, which usually present in childhood.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who has a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa is admitted for nasogastric (NG) feeding, having accepted that she needs to come into hospital. Her BMI is 16.5 on admission. Which of the following is she most at risk of on re-feeding?
explanation:
Hypophosphataemia
Patients with severe malnutrition, including those with anorexia nervosa and a history of alcoholism, are at significant risk of hypophosphataemia when re-feeding is commenced. This is because of reactive hyperinsulinaemia that occurs in response to a carbohydrate load, leading to movement of phosphate into the intracellular space. Hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia are also seen. The electrolyte shifts can precipitate acute muscle weakness including cardiac failure and carry significant morbidity and mortality. Specialist dietician advice is crucial before NG feeding is begun. Key steps include calorie loading at a lower rate, at least initially (50% of total energy requirements for the first few days), and ensuring adequate supplementation of electrolytes such as magnesium, potassium and phosphate as components of the feed or delivered simultaneously IV.

Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is incorrect. Hyponatraemia isn’t associated with the refeeding syndrome. Common causes include fluid retention such as in heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, SIADH, Addison’s disease and use of diuretics.

Hypercalacaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. This condition is not associated with refeeding. Common causes of hypercalcaemia include hyperparathyroidism, malignancies, vitamin D disorders, Paget’s disease and kidneyChat failure. with Hypoglycaemia
Hypoglycaemia is incorrect. The carbohydrate load associated with re-feeding would lead to hyperglycaemia and subsequent insulin release.

Hypochloraemia
Hypochloraemia is incorrect. This would not occur in a patient with the re-feeding syndrome. Common causes of hypochloraemia include severe vomiting and chronic respiratory failure.

stem: You are reviewing the results of a clinical trial thought to impact on flow-mediated dilatation after brachial artery occlusion, a marker of long term vascular risk. The successful production of which compound is best linked to vascular smooth muscle cell relaxation?
explanation:
Nitric oxide
Nitric oxide (NO) is a rapidly diffusible gas with a half-life of only a few seconds. It is formed in endothelial cells via the metabolism of arginine in a reaction catalysed by nitric oxide synthase (NOS). As well as promoting smooth muscle cell relaxation and control of blood pressure, NO has immunological and inflammatory functions. Impaired brachial artery relaxation after a period of occlusion is a sign of endothelial dysfunction and is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. This, at least in part, is due to endothelial damage and reduced NO production. In turn, reduced NO production brings about an increased susceptibility to further endothelial damage.

Angiotensin II
Angiotensin II is incorrect. Angiotensin II promotes vasoconstriction and fibromuscular hyperplasia of arteries, leading to long-term increases in blood pressure.

Endothelin I
Endothelin 1 is incorrect. Endothelin I has a role in vasoconstriction, particularly of the pulmonary vasculature.

Nitrous oxide
Nitrous oxide is incorrect. Nitrous oxide is an inhaled anaesthetic with minimal sedating properties, driving its use in control of pain in labour.

Serotonin
Serotonin is incorrect. Serotonin causes vascular constriction via activation of serotonin S2 receptors. 21.

stem: Which one of the following, when seen in a pregnant woman, is not likely to be physiological?
explanation:
Persistent haematuria
Persistent haematuria is not a feature of normal pregnancy and may indicate renal vasculitis or underlying urinary tract infection.

Glycosuria
Glycosuria (Option A) is incorrect. There is reduced renal reabsorption of glucose in pregnancy, glycosuria may therefore in some cases be a normal finding. Persistent glycosuria should, however, be investigated to rule out gestational diabetes.

Ketonuria
Ketonuria (Option C) is incorrect. Ketonuria may be seen in normal pregnancy, related to hyperemesis or periods of low carbohydrate intake.

Urine osmolality 130
Urine osmolality 130 (Option D) is incorrect. A urine osmolality of 130 is in the normal range.

Urine specific gravity 1.01.

stem: What is the anion gap?
explanation:
15 mEq/l
Calculating the anion gap is clinically useful because it helps in the differential diagnosis of a number of disease states. The anion gap is the difference between measured cations and measured anions. A raised anion gap suggests the presence of unmeasured anions. The simplified calculation (which omits potassium) to find the anion gap is that the gap is equal to [Na +] - ([Cl -] + [HCO 3 -]) (all units mmol/l). The normal range is 8–16 mEq/l. Therefore, [140]-[105+20] = 15

5 mEq/l
5 mEq/l is incorrect. A common cause of a low anion gap is hypoalbuminemia. Albumin is a negatively charged protein, low albumin will therefore cause the retention of negatively charged anions chloride and bicarbonate. This will result in a decreased anion gap.

10 mEq/l
10 mEq/l is incorrect. In patients with a pathology related normal anion gap the cause will be a drop in bicarbonate. This must be compensated for by an increase in Chloride casing a hyperchloremic acidosis. A normal anion gap may be a normal variant, or indicate loss of bicarbonate ions (diarrhoea), recovery from DKA, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, parenteral nutrition and renal tubular acidosis.

30 mEq/l
30 mEq/l is incorrect. A raised anion gap suggests the presence of unmeasured anions. Causes include: Lactate Ketones/ Diabtetic ketoacidosis (likely in this scenario) Methanol, ethylene glycol Kidney disease/rhabdomyolysis Uremia Salicylates

0 mEq/l
0 mEq/l 0mEq/l is incorrect.

stem: A 17-year-old phenotypic female with no clinical evidence of dysmorphism is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for the investigation of primary amenorrhoea. On examination, breast development is normal, the external genitalia are normal female in appearance but pubic hair is sparse. Her karyotype is found to be 46XY. A defect in which one of the following is most likely to be causing this presentation?
explanation:
The androgen receptor
A combination of female phenotype on external examination with 46XY karyotype is typical of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Masculinisation may occur at puberty due to increased testosterone secretion.

Conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
Conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone is incorrect. Failure of conversion of testosterone to Chat in with dihydrotestosterone (DHT), due to 5α-reductase deficiency, in a 46XY individual usually results an ambiguous phenotype (the development of the male external genitalia in utero is largely dependent on DHT)

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) secretion
FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) secretion is incorrect. Phenotypic women with low FSH, for example due to ovarian failure, may have primary amenorrhoea, but the 46XY karyotype would not be found.

Prolactin secretion
Prolactin secretion is incorrect. Deficient prolactin secretion is usually due to general anterior pituitary dysfunction and thus other hormonal defects would also be seen. Rarer isolated prolactin deficiency may have a genetic basis, but not involving the 46XY karyotype.

Testosterone secretion
Testosterone secretion is incorrect. A failure of testosterone secretion alone in a 46XY individual also usually results in an ambiguous phenotype.

stem: An otherwise well 62-year-old woman with hypertension is referred to the Outpatient Clinic for assessment. Despite treatment with a thiazide diuretic, a ß-adrenergic antagonist (ß-blocker) and an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, her blood pressure is 158/92 mmHg. Investigations show serum sodium concentration is 138 mmol/l, serum potassium concentration 3.2 mmol/l, serum creatinine concentration 108 μmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the hypokalaemia?
explanation:
The thiazide diuretic
Thiazides cause hypokalaemia through increasing the delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule where sodium is reabsorbed and potassium excreted.

A low dietary potassium intake
A low dietary potassium intake with A low dietary potassium intake is incorrect. Most normal diets contain adequate amounts ofChat potassium.

Excessive secretion of aldosterone
Excessive secretion of aldosterone is incorrect. Whilst increased aldosterone secretion does cause increased potassium excretion and hypokalaemia, hyporeninaemic hyper-aldosteronism is a much less common cause of hypertension versus other causes such as essential hypertension or renovascular disease.

The ACE inhibitor
The ACE inhibitor is incorrect. Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors tend to raise plasma potassium concentration.

The ß-adrenergic antagonist
The ß-adrenergic antagonist is incorrect. ß-blockers also tend to raise plasma potassium concentration.

stem: You are doing a stint as the chemical pathology reviewer for the local hospital. You are doing random quality control on the results. Which one of the following sets of results is most likely to be the result of an analytical error?
options: pH 7.38; pO 2 13.2 kPa; pCO 2 3.9 kPa; bicarbonate 17 mmol/l
pH 7.2; pO 2 13.8 kPa; pCO 2 3.0 kPa; bicarbonate 24 mmol/l
pH 7.4; pO 2 12.5 kPa; pCO 2 5.4 kPa; bicarbonate 22 mmol/l
pH 7.35; pO 2 9.6 kPa; pCO 2 7.0 kPa; bicarbonate 32 mmol/l
pH 7.45; pO 2 13.5 kPa; pCO 2 3.4 kPa; bicarbonate 18 mmol/l
explanation:
pH 7.2; pO 2 13.8 kPa; pCO 2 3.0 kPa; bicarbonate 24 mmol/l
The pCO 2 is low and bicarbonate is in the normal range, which is consistent with a respiratory alkalosis; however, the pH is 7.2, which is inconsistent

pH 7.38; pO 2 13.2 kPa; pCO 2 3.9 kPa; bicarbonate 17 mmol/l
pH 7.38; pO 2 13.2 kPa; pCO 2 3.9 kPa; bicarbonate 17 mmol/l pH 7.38; pO 2 13.2 kPa; pCO 23.9 kPa; bicarbonate 17 mmol/l is incorrect. This stem is not the correct answer as within this stem is a low pCO 2 and a slightly reduced bicarbonate; hence, the virtually normal pH value is consistent with this.

pH 7.4; pO 2 12.5 kPa; pCO 2 5.4 kPa; bicarbonate 22 mmol/l
pH 7.4; pO 2 12.5 kPa; pCO 2 5.4 kPa; bicarbonate 22 mmol/l is incorrect. This result is consistent with an absolutely normal blood gas, again no reason to suspect an analytical error.

pH 7.35; pO 2 9.6 kPa; pCO 2 7.0 kPa; bicarbonate 32 mmol/l
pH 7.35; pO 2 9.6 kPa; pCO 2 7.0 kPa; bicarbonate 32 mmol/l is incorrect. With a raised CO2 and bicarbonate but normal pH, indicate a compensated respiratory acidosis, likely due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease i.e. no reason to suspect an error.

pH 7.45; pO 2 13.5 kPa; pCO 2 3.4 kPa; bicarbonate 18 mmol/l
pH 7.45; pO 2 13.5 kPa; pCO 2 3.4 kPa; bicarbonate 18 mmol/l is incorrect.

stem: You are interested in a device that measures pulse pressure as a screening tool for cardiovascular disease. You are aware that pulse pressure increases with increasing age. Which of the following contributes most to increased pulse pressure?
explanation:
Decreased aortic compliance
Decreased aortic compliance with increasing age means that the aorta is less able to absorb the pulse wave that comes from left ventricular contraction, increasing pulse pressure

Decreased left ventricular wall compliance
Decreased left ventricular wall compliance is incorrect. Decreased LV wall compliance contributes to diastolic dysfunction via impaired diastolic relaxation rather than pulse pressure.

Decreased peripheral vascular resistance
Decreased peripheral vascular resistance is incorrect. Peripheral vascular resistance increases with age rather than decreases.

Increased aortic compliance
Increased aortic compliance is incorrect. Aortic compliance decreases not increases with age, as seen in the correct answer.

Increased peripheral vascular resistance.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after suffering a blackout. She was waiting for the bus when she felt nauseated, dizzy and sweaty. She lost consciousness for 1 min. A friend says she was pale, had some jerking of her limbs for 10 s, but did not bite her tongue and there was no history of urinary incontinence. She recovered immediately with no confusion or disorientation. Examination is normal. ECG is normal. What further investigations are required to make a diagnosis?
explanation:
No investigations
The patient has had a blackout. The most likely diagnosis is a vasovagal syncope. It is usually preceded by dizziness, feeling hot, nausea and darkening of vision. The syncope lasts for a short period (up to 1 minute). There are some jerking movements of the limbs due to brain hypoperfusion. Tongue biting does not occur and the patient recovers quickly. Common predisposing factors are pain, prolonged standing, a hot environment and a heavy meal. No investigations are needed apart, perhaps, from an ECG in typical case. The history gives the diagnosis.

CT brain
CT brain is incorrect. Vasovagal syncope is a clinical diagnosis and all investigations will be negative.

Doppler of carotids
Doppler of carotids is incorrect. Vasovagal syncope is a clinical diagnosis and all investigations will be negative.

EEG
EEG is incorrect. Vasovagal syncope is a clinical diagnosis and all investigations will be negative.

MRI brain.

stem: A 58-year-old patient is reviewed 2 weeks after discharge from a prolonged hospital stay, when a road traffic collision resulted in multiple rib fractures, complicated by the development of a left sided pneumonia. On review in the clinic he appears to be recovering. His BP is 122/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. There is residual left sided chest bruising, but air entry is normal on both sides. He has lost a few kg in weight since his admission. Which of the following are you likely to find on hormone testing?
explanation:
Elevated cortisol
Acute phase proteins and some hormones increase markedly post-injury. Serum cortisol significantly increases immediately post-injury and remains elevated for around three weeks before returning to normal levels.

Elevated catecholamines
Elevated catecholamines withof Elevated catecholamines is incorrect. Whilst catecholamines may be raised during the acuteChat phase stress, around the time of the accident, it is unlikely at this stage that they would still be elevated.

Elevated thyroxine
Elevated thyroxine is incorrect. During a period of severe non-thyroidal illness, T3 and T4 are reduced rather than elevated, the phenomenon known as sick euthyroid syndrome.

Elevated aldosterone
Elevated aldosterone is incorrect. Aldosterone is likely to be raised immediately following the event, but should have normalised at this stage after injury.

Elevated growth hormone.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department by her daughter. Her daughter is very concerned, as her mother has developed nausea, vomiting, pyrexia and confusion after spending the day sitting out in the sun with her family. On examination, she is pyrexial (38.0°C), her BP is 110/72 mmHg, pulse is 88/min and regular and she looks dehydrated. Which of the following physiological changes is likely to have increased her risk of heat stroke?
explanation:
Decreased sweating
A number of physiological changes occur in the elderly, but the one that is most associated with increased risk of heat stroke is loss of the ability to sweat effectively.

Decreased peripheral dilatation
Decreased peripheral dilatation is incorrect. Increasing age is associated with increased arteriolar calcification, which may partially reduce the ability to lose heat by peripheral vasodilation, although at a Chat muchwith lesser extent compared to decreased sweating.

Increased basal metabolic rate
Increased basal metabolic rate is incorrect. The ageing process leads to a decreased basal metabolic rate, and decreased energy expenditure.

Increased sweating
Increased sweating is incorrect. The elderly are somewhat affected by decreased ability to sweat effectively. Increased sweating would help maintain homeostatic body temperatures and resist the effects of heat stroke.

Increased peripheral vasodilatation.

stem: A 22-year-old woman was noted by her boyfriend to have multiple episodes of collapse. It occurred six times in a 1-week period, always when the patient was standing. Each time the patient would look pale and collapse abruptly with her eyes closed. After approximately 2 min as measured by her boyfriend, the patient would wake up and feel weak, remembering a dizzy feeling and a sensation of 'vision going black' before collapsing. There was no confusion after the attack and the patient was well between attacks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vasovagal syncope
Vasovagal syncope is the most likely diagnosis here. The typical prodrome (light-headedness, ‘closing down’ of vision), brief loss of consciousness and immediate orientation post-attack is entirely in keeping with this.

Atonic epileptic seizure
Atonic epileptic seizure is incorrect. Atonic seizure is a rare form of epileptic seizure presenting as sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone, usually without warning, which causes the patient to fall, often sustaining trauma, especially to the head. This would not be associated with the prodrome described here.

Cardiogenic syncope
Cardiogenic syncope is incorrect. This patient is young, with a postural pattern to the attacks and with no prior history of arrhythmia, so cardiogenic syncope is less likely (although it should always be considered). In addition, she describes clear presyncopal symptoms, which are typical in vasovagal cases.

Complex partial seizure
Complex partial seizure is incorrect. As described, the features in this case are typical of vasovagal syncope. ‘Red flags’ for complex partial seizures would include symptoms such as intense déjà vu, a rising abdominal sensation and witnesses describing distal limb or oromasticatory automatism.

Non-epileptic attack.

stem: Which cell type produces surfactant?
explanation:
Type II pneumocyte
Phospholipid molecules that reduce surface tension in the alveolar air–liquid interface are called surfactant. Surfactant is produced in conjunction with proteins from alveolar type II epithelial cells (type II pneumocytes) lying free in the alveolar spaces against alveolar walls.

Alveolar macrophage
Alveolar macrophage is incorrect. Surfactant is produced in conjunction with proteins from alveolar type II epithelial cells (type II pneumocytes) lying free in the alveolar spaces against alveolar walls.

Endothelial cell
Endothelial cell is incorrect. Surfactant is produced in conjunction with proteins from alveolar type II epithelial cells (type II pneumocytes) lying free in the alveolar spaces against alveolar walls.

Goblet cell
Goblet cell is incorrect. Surfactant is produced in conjunction with proteins from alveolar type II epithelial cells (type II pneumocytes) lying free in the alveolar spaces against alveolar walls.

Type I pneumocyte.

stem: A 24-year-old man, a new immigrant to the UK from Eastern Europe who had worked in his own country as a demolition contractor, undergoes a medical examination and is found to have glycosuria. His blood lead concentration is high. Which one of the following findings would suggest that he has a generalised disorder of proximal tubular function?
explanation:
Metabolic acidosis
Bicarbonate is normally totally reabsorbed from the glomerular filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule. Decreased bicarbonate absorption causes metabolic acidosis (type-2 renal tubular acidosis); however, the urine can be acidified as: The plasma bicarbonate concentration (and hence the bicarbonate load for reabsorption) falls Distal tubular secretion of hydrogen ions is intact.

Albuminuria
Albuminuria is incorrect. Proximal tubular damage can be associated with proteinuria, but generally with low molecular weight proteins that are filtered by the glomerulus (ie smaller than albumin).

Hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia is incorrect. Generalised proximal tubular dysfunction will lead to reduced potassium reabsorption and hence hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia.

Inability to acidify the urine
Inability to acidify the urine is incorrect. Urine is acidified as the plasma bicarbonate concentration (and hence the bicarbonate load for reabsorption) falls therefore leading to less bicarbonate in the urine, and distal tubular secretion of hydrogen ions is intact allowing for greater acidification.

Increased serum urea concentration.

stem: A 24-year-old man is being provided with long-term parenteral nutrition for Crohn’s disease. His energy requirement is estimated to be approximately 2500 kcal/24 h. Which one of the following combinations of lipid emulsion and dextrose solutions would be most appropriate to provide his energy requirements?
explanation:
Dextrose 50% 750 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml
Dextrose 50% and 20% lipid emulsions each provide about 2000 kcal/l. 1. His requirements would thus be met by a combined total of about 1250 ml of these fluids, making dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 750 ml or dextrose 50% 750 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml an appropriate amount of energy. The other combinations either provide too much or too little energy. 1. Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml provides too little energy (~2000 kcal). 2. Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 1000 ml provides too much energy, as does dextrose 50% 1000 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml (~3000 kcal). Lipid should provide not more than half the total energy requirements. 1. Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 750 ml, would provide 60%, which is too high. 2. Dextrose 50% 750 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml provides 40%, making this an appropriate regimen.

Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml
Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml is incorrect. This combination provides too little energy (~2000 kcal).

Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 750 ml
Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 750 ml is incorrect. This combination has too much of the energy requirement provided by lipids (~60%, when it should be no more than 50%).

Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 1000 ml
Dextrose 50% 500 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 1000 ml is incorrect. This combination provides too much energy (~3000 kcal).

Dextrose 50% 1000 ml, lipid emulsion 20% 500 ml.

stem: A 40-year-old man with known chronic liver disease presents with exertional dyspnoea. On examination his blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg and his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is slightly elevated. He has bilateral pleural effusions, ascites and marked pitting oedema, for which his GP has prescribed furosemide. Investigations reveal: plasma sodium 136 mmol/l, K + 3.5 mmol/l, bicarbonate 30 mmol/l and chloride 99 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most characteristic physiological activity that results in retention of sodium in the face of salt and water overload?
options: Decrease in pressure and volume receptors
explanation:
Arterial underfilling
This man has chronic liver disease, and in cirrhosis, arterial vasodilatation due to nitric oxide overactivity, coupled with hypoalbuminemia, which drives low colloid osmotic pressure, leads to arterial underfilling.

Activation of the parasympathetic system
Activation of the parasympathetic system is incorrect. There is consequent activation of the sympathetic system.

Decrease in pressure and volume receptors
Decrease in pressure and volume receptors is incorrect. This is perceived by the pressure and volume receptors as hypovolaemia.

Increase atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) levels
Increase atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) levels is incorrect. When there is triggering of pressure and volume receptors as hypovolaemia, there is decreased release of atrial natriuretic peptides (ANP). ANPs are secreted in response to stretching of the atrial wall, reduced sympathetic simulation of β-adrenoceptors, hypernatraemia, angiotensin II, endothelin and exercise. It acts to reduce sodium and water retention, thereby reducing blood pressure, and has opposite functions to aldosterone secreted by the zona glomerulosa.

Inhibition of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release.

stem: You are called to see a 56-year-old man 2 h after a cardiac catheterisation. He is actively bleeding from his catheter site and his dressings and bedclothes are soaked with blood. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Anuria is pathognomonic of grade III shock
Grade I shock applies with up to a 20% loss of circulating blood volume
Grade IV shock is seen with a 30% loss of circulating blood volume
Loss of 2 l of blood is consistent with normal systolic blood pressure
The pulse can remain normal in patients with grade I shock
explanation:
The pulse can remain normal in patients with grade I shock
As per ATLS shock classification: Grade I shock - Loss of up to 15% (750 ml) of blood volume (not 20%); blood pressure is normal but there may be a slight tachycardia (note only may be) Grade II shock - 15–30% (750 ml to 1.5 l) blood-volume loss, systolic blood pressure is usually normal but a tachycardia is present Grade III shock - 30–40% (1.5–2 l) loss, hypotension, tachycardia and fall in urine output seen (usually, complete anuria is unlikely) Grade IV shock - > 40% (> 2 l) blood-volume loss (not 30%), anuria and severe shock observed The grading of shock according to percentage blood loss has lost validity in recent years, with increasing recognition that the distinction between classes is somewhat arbitrary with significant individual variation. Regardless, it is still examined and provides some guidance as to shock severity. In particular it illustrates that significant blood loss is possible without hypotension – an important fact to remember when resuscitating the bleeding patient.

Anuria is pathognomonic of grade III shock
Anuria is pathognomonic of grade III shock is incorrect. While a fall in urine output is seen in grade III shock, complete anuria is unlikely, and is observed in grade IV shock.

Grade I shock applies with up to a 20% loss of circulating blood volume
Grade I shock applies with up to a 20% loss of circulating blood volume is incorrect. Grade I shock applies with up to a 15% loss of blood volume, not 20%.

Grade IV shock is seen with a 30% loss of circulating blood volume
Grade IV shock is seen with a 30% loss of circulating blood volume is incorrect. Grade IV shock is seen with a loss of blood volume in excess of 40%.

Loss of 2 l of blood is consistent with normal systolic blood pressure.

stem: A 52-year-old man weighing 70kg is commenced on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) post elective extensive bowel resection on a background of a malignancy. In the run up to the surgery he was clinically well. Which one of the following most accurately represents appropriate nitrogen requirements (g N/kg per day) and calorie requirements (kcal/kg per day) when drawing up a TPN regime for this patient?
options: Nitrogen requirement 0.15 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 25 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 15 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 25 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 35 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.2 g N/kg/day, calorie requirement 15 kcal/kg/day
explanation:
Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 35 kcal/kg per day
TPN requirements depend on the clinical state of the patient and the reason TPN is required. Given the extensive resection of tissue involved in bowel resection, this falls under the classification of severe injury. Usual ranges for nutritional requirements are given in the table below: Condition Nitrogen requirement (g N/kg per day) Calorie requirement (kcal/kg per day) Reduced food intake 0.15-0.2 25-30 Moderate injury/sepsis 0.2-0.3 30-35 Severe injury/sepsis 0.3-0.35 35-40

Nitrogen requirement 0.15 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 25 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.15 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 25 kcal/kg per day is incorrect. This would be approprate in cases of reduced food intake, rather than following major abdominal surgery.

Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 15 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 15 kcal/kg per day is incorrect, this regime would be more suitable in patients with sepsis. This patient would require a higher calorie intake.

Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day, calorie requirement 25 kcal/kg per day
Nitrogen requirement 0.3 g N/kg per day is correct, but the calorie intake would not be sufficient for this patient.

Nitrogen requirement 0.2 g N/kg/day, calorie requirement 15 kcal/kg/day.

stem: A patient on enteral nutrition develops constipation. What could explain the underlying clinical physiology?
explanation:
Inadequate fluid replacement
Inadequate fluid replacement can lead to constipation in patients receiving enteral nutrition. Diarrhoea is common in enteral feeding. The following all explain diarrhoea in patients receiving enteral nutrition: hyperosmolar feed bacterial contamination low feed temperature reduced intestinal absorptive capacity too rapid or irregular administration lactose intolerance.

Bacterial contamination
Bacterial contamination is incorrect. Bacterial contamination is likely to lead to diarrhoea in enteral feeding.

Hyperosmolar feed
Hyperosmolar feed is incorrect. Hyperosmolar feed is likely to lead to diarrhoea in enteral feeding.

Low feed temperature
Low feed temperature is incorrect. Low feed temperature is likely to lead to diarrhoea in enteral feeding.

Reduced intestinal absorptive capacity.

stem: A patient’s respiratory function is evaluated before lung resection (for a tumour), both at rest and with exertion. Which one of the following takes place during inspiration at rest?
options: A reduction in intrathoracic pressure of 1–3 mmHg is created
The diaphragm drops by 10 cm during normal breathing
explanation:
A reduction in intrathoracic pressure of 1–3 mmHg is created
During normal breathing the diaphragm may drop 1 cm, creating an intrathoracic pressure drop of 1–3 mmHg and an air intake of 500 ml.

Abdominal muscles contract
Abdominal muscles contract is incorrect. Abdominal muscles are involved in active expiration.

Accessory muscles relax
Accessory muscles relax is incorrect. The accessory muscles relax during passive expiration.

The diaphragm drops by 10 cm during normal breathing
The diaphragm drops by 10 cm during normal breathing is incorrect. A drop of 10 cm is more in keeping with exercise. During strenuous exercise the diaphragm may drop 10 cm, producing an intrathoracic pressure drop of 100 mmHg and an air intake of 3000 ml.

The rib cage recoils.

stem: A 41-year-old patient complains of a persistent ringing in the right ear, which no one else can hear. You presume a diagnosis of tinnitus. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the clinical physiology of the ear?
options: High-frequency waves are detected in the scala tympani
Low-frequency waves are detected in the scala vestibuli
Normal hearing frequency only ranges from 20 to 2000 Hz
The scala media contains the organ of Corti
The scala media is filled with perilymph
explanation:
The scala media contains the organ of Corti
The scala media contains the organ of Corti, which produces nerve impulses in response to sound vibrations.

High-frequency waves are detected in the scala tympani
High-frequency waves are detected in the scala tympani is incorrect. High-frequency waves are detected in the scala vestibuli (base of the cochlea), not tympani (the apex of the cochlea).

Low-frequency waves are detected in the scala vestibuli
Low-frequency waves are detected in the scala vestibuli is incorrect. Low-frequency waves are detected in the scala tympani, not vestibuli. Both contain perilymph.

Normal hearing frequency only ranges from 20 to 2000 Hz
Normal hearing frequency only ranges from 20 to 2000 Hz is incorrect. Normal hearing frequency ranges from 20 to 20 000 Hz, not 2000.

The scala media is filled with perilymph.

stem: While treating a diabetic patient who is controlled with insulin you perform fundoscopy and find new vessel disease in the macula lutea. Which one of the following is true of ocular physiology?
options: As it corresponds with the blind spot, retinopathy will have less functional effect on acuity
The central portion of the macula is known as the fovea centralis
The macula is rich in rods
There is a direct relationship between proliferative retinopathy and the frequency of cataracts
This corresponds with the optic papilla
explanation:
The central portion of the macula is known as the fovea centralis
The fovea centralis has the highest acuity and is central in the macula.

As it corresponds with the blind spot, retinopathy will have less functional effect on acuity
As it corresponds with the blind spot, retinopathy will have less functional effect on acuity is incorrect. The disease in the macula, containing the fovea centralis, will certainly impact acuity.

The macula is rich in rods
The macula is rich in rods is incorrect. The macula is rich in cones, not rods

There is a direct relationship between proliferative retinopathy and the frequency of cataracts
There is a direct relationship between proliferative retinopathy and the frequency of cataracts is incorrect. There is no direct relationship between proliferative retinopathy and the frequency of cataracts.

This corresponds with the optic papilla.

stem: An 25-year-old woman is found to be hypertensive. Her creatinine is 220 µmol/l, and urine dipstick testing shows blood ++. Her mother had also been hypertensive and had died prematurely of a cerebral haemorrhage aged 43 years. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s hypertension?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Approximately 6% of patients have an identifiable cause for hypertension, of which the most common is renal impairment. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease invariably causes hypertension and non-visible haematuria, which may be detected before elevation of the plasma creatinine. A family history is usual, and cerebral haemorrhage is an important association.

Essential hypertension
Essential hypertension is incorrect. Essential hypertension would not present with the haematuria. Prevalence of essential hypertension increases with age, and individuals with hypertension at younger ages are more likely to be due to secondary causes.

Fibromuscular dysplasia
Fibromuscular dysplasia is incorrect. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory disease of the blood vessels. It may affect any arterial bed, but the most commonly affected are the renal and carotid arteries. There may be a family history. However, haematuria is not seen and a renal bruit may be audible.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. Dipstick haematuria may suggest glomerulonephritis as a differential. IgA nephropathy would be the most common glomerulonephritis to cause this and often presents in exactly this way. However, the family history and cerebral haemorrhage could not be explained by IgA nephropathy.

Renovascular disease.

stem: A competitive cyclist tests positive for the banned performance-enhancing drug EPO. What is the mechanism of action of erythropoietin when used as a performance-enhancing drug?
explanation:
Improvement of exercise tolerance
Erythropoietin increases red cell mass in the human body Increased red cell mass and therefore oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood delivers more oxygen to exercising muscles, improving exercise tolerance Benefits can last for weeks, but it can be detected only for a few days EPO may have been implicated in the deaths of a number of young athletes, particularly cycling

Improvement of blood pressure control
Improvement of blood pressure control is incorrect. Whilst EPO is often associated with hypertension in medical administration; this would not offer a performance advantage.

Improvement of renal function
Improvement of renal function is incorrect. Whilst EPO is often indicated in kidney disease to manage anaemia, there is no direct effect on renal function.

Increase in muscle mass
Increase in muscle mass is incorrect. There is no direct effect on muscle mass.

Reduction in pain.

stem: You are researching a new agent for the management of hypoxia related to acute pneumonia. Part of the assessment includes changes in the pulmonary vasculature in response to hypoxia. When considering acute hypoxia, which one of the following is true of the pulmonary vasculature?
options: An area of lung affected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasodilatation
An area of lung unaffected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasodilatation
An area of lung unaffected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasoconstriction
Hypothermia promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction in the affected area of lung
Increased cardiac output promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction in the affected area of lung
explanation:
An area of lung unaffected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasodilatation
When an area of lung is affected by hypoxia, but CO2 is not raised, a process of shunting occurs, i.e. Vasodilatation occurs in areas of lung where gas exchange is better; i.e. where there is no pneumonia.

An area of lung affected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasodilatation
An area of lung affected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasodilatation is incorrect. Vasoconstriction restricts the blood supply to the poorly oxygenated areas of the lung with pneumonia (not vasodilation).

An area of lung unaffected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasoconstriction
An area of lung unaffected by pneumonia is likely to experience vasoconstriction is incorrect as unaffected lung experiences vasodilation not constriction. This in effect increases the functional part of the lung available for gas exchange.

Hypothermia promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction in the affected area of lung
Hypothermia promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction in the affected area of lung is incorrect. Hypothermia inhibits this vasoconstrictive process rather than promotes it.

Increased cardiac output promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction in the affected area of lung.

stem: You are reviewing a study which seeks to measure troponin I to estimate the level of cardiac myonecrosis. Where in the cardiac myocyte is troponin present?
options: In the area adjacent to the thick myofilaments
In the area adjacent to the thin myofilaments
explanation:
In the area adjacent to the thin myofilaments
Troponin binds to the actin in thin myofilaments, forming a complex between G-actin and tropomyosin. Both troponin I and troponin T are also found in skeletal muscle though cardiac troponin I differs slightly from that found in skeletal muscle. Troponin T has less structural homology with that found in skeletal muscle. Very specific assays for troponin T in particular have now almost completely replaced assessment of creatine kinase in myocardial infarction.

Free within the cytoplasm
Free within the cytoplasm is incorrect. Free troponin is not physiological but suggests damage and leak.

In mitochondria
In mitochondria is incorrect. Troponin is not found in the mitochondria.

In the area adjacent to the thick myofilaments
In the area adjacent to the thick myofilaments is incorrect. Troponin binds to the thin, not thick filaments.

In T-tubules.

stem: You are giving advice on healthy lifestyle choices to a 35-year-old man who is looking to reduce his weight. In addition to advice around increasing activity levels and reducing alcohol consumption, you also discuss monitoring and reducing calorie consumption. Which of the following food items has the highest calorie load per gram?
explanation:
Cheddar cheese
The correct answer is Cheddar cheese (Option A). Per gram, fat is the highest calorie food source at 9 kilocalories per gram. In contrast, carbohydrates and proteins have a lower energy content at 4 kilocalories per gram. Cheddar cheese is approximately 70% fat, 25% protein and 2% carbohydrate, i.e. it contains the highest proportion of fat and thus the most calories.

Lean red meat
Lean red meat (Option B) is incorrect. Lean red meat is predominantly protein i.e. 4 kilocalories/gram.

Pasta
Pasta (Option C) is incorrect. Pasta is predominantly carbohydrate i.e. 4 kilocalories/gram.

Sugar
Sugar (Option D) is incorrect. Sugar is predominantly carbohydrate i.e. 4 kilocalories/gram. It is important to be mindful however that a balanced diet should not rely too heavily on sugary foods and refined carbohydrates such as in white bread; proteins and healthy fats are essential.

White bread.

stem: Aquaporin 2 gene mutation is likely to cause which of the following disorders?
explanation:
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
The aquaporin 2 channel is responsible for reabsorption of water from glomerular filtrate in response to ADH. Gene mutations in the aquaporin 2 gene are recognised in association with congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Cranial diabetes insipidus
Cranial diabetes insipidus is incorrect. Cranial diabetes insipidus in contrast would imply a central deficit in ADH production, not a lack of renal response to ADH.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus encompasses the metabolic disorders involving hyperglycaemia due to lack of insulin, or insulin resistance.

DIDMOAD syndrome
DIDMOAD syndrome is incorrect. The DIDMOAD syndrome is a mitochondrial disorder associated with diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, optic atrophy and deafness.

Primary polydipsia.
